/ai-files.t: How-to guide Use the tool files with your AI Every Praxis tool comes as a file you can give to your own AI. Drop it into your folder, start a chat and your AI walks you through the same steps as the tool on the site. Updated. October 2026 Time needed. About 5 minutes Works with. Claude, ChatGPT, Codex, Mistral, Gemini, Copilot Step 01

Each tool has a button at the top marked "Download for your AI (.md)". They're also on your dashboard at tutto.one/learn, next to each tool. Tool File On the site AI charter. Download (.md). Web version. Agent scorecard. Download (.md). Web version. Hand-over check. Download (.md). Web version. Use case card. Download (.md). Web version. VS Code setup pack. Download (.md). Web version. A.md file is plain text with a little formatting. Each one has two parts: a short note for you at the top, and the instructions your AI follows to run the tool. Step 02

/ai-files.h: Put them in your working folder
/ai-files.t: Keep the files where your AI works, so it can read them whenever you need them. Open your working folder in VS Code (step 2 of the setup guide shows how). Drag the downloaded files from your Downloads folder onto the Explorer on the left. They appear in the list with the rest of your files, as in Fig. 1. Click one to read it. To see it formatted, choose Markdown Preview from the menu at the top right of the file. Step 03

The path tells your AI exactly which file to read. 1 2 Fig. 1 The files sit in your folder like any other. Right-click the one you want. 1 The tool file, dropped into the working folder. Here it is praxis-agent-scorecard.md. 2 Copy Path. Shortcut ⌥⌘C on a Mac, Shift+Alt+C on Windows. Step 04

/ai-files.h: Start a chat and say what you want
/ai-files.t: Open the AI panel on the right, start a new chat, paste the path and say in a sentence or two what you want to make with it. 1 2 3 Fig. 2 Paste the path, then say what you want to make. 1 The path you copied, pasted on the first line. 2 Your request in your own words. Here: use the scorecard kit to make a translation agent that weighs meaning over literal wording. 3 Send. Say what you're working on. The file is enough to start, but a line about your real task means your AI tailors its suggestions from the first question. Not using VS Code? In Claude, ChatGPT, Le Chat, Gemini or Copilot, open a new chat, attach the file with the paperclip or + button (or paste everything in it), and send Let's start with a line about your task. Everything else works the same. Step 05

It runs the same steps as the tool on the site: one step at a time, with suggestions and the same documents at the end. 1 Fig. 3 Your AI reads the file and starts the first step. 1 It says what you will finish with, picks up your request and asks the first step's questions, with suggestions you can say yes to or change. 1 2 Fig. 4 It keeps track of what is done and what is still open. 1 The checklist from the tool. It ticks items off as you answer. 2 Answer in short. Tell it when something doesn't apply to your task. Short answers are fine: "yes", "2 and 4", "skip". You can go back to any step by saying so. If your AI can create documents, it offers to put the final result in one. If not, it writes it out in the chat for you to copy. Step 06

Answer the questions and let your AI guide you through. Tell it if parts aren't relevant to your task. Then test the result, ideally on something where you already know the answer. Showing it what good work looks like beats describing it, and doing both gives you the best results. Keep a couple of finished pieces of real work to hand, and ask your AI to check its output against them. Your answers stay in your AI's chat, under that tool's terms. Leave out personal or confidential details unless your organisation has approved the tool. If your agent can act on its own, keep it on the mode that asks before it acts (Manual in Claude, Ask in Mistral) until you trust it

/bi-github.t: Praxis programme · Handout · GitHub. One repository or several? A few of you are already building tools you want to share. GitHub keeps every version and lets several people work on the same files. The first question is whether everything goes in one place or each tool gets its own. Read this before you set up your accounts We go through it together in January Four words you'll need. One repository or several. What we'll set up. When a tool gets its own. Your account. Bring your project in

That's all the vocabulary. Claude does the rest when you ask in plain words. Repository. A project folder that remembers every version of every file, and who changed what. Organisation. Background Italia's own space on GitHub. It holds your repositories and decides who sees each one. Save and share. Keeps a version with a one-line reason and sends it to GitHub, so the others get it. Get latest. Brings everyone else's changes onto your computer. Do it each time you start

Both work. They suit different stages. One team repository. bi-ai/ CLAUDE.md library/ instructions, scorecards tools/ media-screening/ registry-chart/ translation/ One thing to set up, one place to look. Tools reuse the library and each other. "Get latest" once and you have it all. Everyone in it sees everything. Gets crowded as it grows. One repository per tool. bi-library/ media-screening/ registry-chart/ translation/ each with its own CLAUDE.md, its own people and history You choose who sees each tool. A tool can run online or go to a client on its own. A clear history per tool. More to set up and remember. The library has to be linked into each one

/bi-github.h: What we'll set up: start with one
/bi-github.t: A team of your size, with tools that are a few weeks old, is better off in one repository. Each tool gets a folder. A tool moves into its own repository when it needs to, and keeps its history when it does. Your project on your laptop A colleague's project on theirs Riccardo's files team library bi-ai library/ and tools/, one folder per tool Client documents stay on the shared drive, never on GitHub The organisation belongs to Background Italia. I join while we work together and leave when you're ready. Two of you are owners, so it never depends on one person

/bi-github.h: When a tool gets its own repository
/bi-github.t: If none of these is true, the tool stays a folder. If one is, ask Claude to move it out. Different people. Only some of you should see it, or a freelancer needs it and nothing else. It runs on its own. It becomes a website, a service or something on the office machine. It leaves the firm. You hand it to a client or a partner. It's slowing everyone down. Big files, or lots of changes nobody else needs. To move a tool out Move tools/media-screening into its own repository in our organisation, with its history. Give it a CLAUDE.md that points to our library, then remove the folder here and say where it went in the README

Ten minutes each. Use your work email. Sign up at github.com with your Background Italia email. The free plan is all you need. Add a passkey under Settings, Password and authentication. It's your fingerprint or face, so no extra code to type. Send Alice your username. She adds you to the organisation and you accept the email. Sign in to VS Code with GitHub: the person icon at the bottom left

Keep working where you are until the repository exists. Then each of you brings one project in, with Claude checking it first. Put the repository in a plain folder such as Documents/GitHub. Not in Google Drive, OneDrive, Dropbox or iCloud: the sync and GitHub both write to the same hidden files and damage each other. Once, to get the team repository Clone our team repository bi-ai into Documents/GitHub and open it. Then, for your project Copy my project from <paste the path> into tools/<tool name>/. Before you save anything, check it for client names, personal details, passwords, API keys and files over 50 MB, and show me what you found. Write a short README.md: what the tool does, how to start it and who looks after it. Then save and share with the message "Add <tool name>". If Claude finds something, it goes on the shared drive or on the list of files GitHub ignores, and the tool reads it from there. Every day after that Get latest. And when you're done: "Save and share: <what you changed>". If two of you changed the same lines, Claude says so and suggests how to combine them. Read it, then say which version to keep

/bi-session-4.t: Praxis programme · Session 4 · Brief it once. Write it down once, so it's right every time What we covered on Wednesday, built around the work you brought: Gabriel's report from Spain and Alice and Riccardo's Italy and France job. Keep it open while you set up your folders this week. Wed 4 November 2026, session 4 of 8 Next: Wed 11 November, 11:00 to 12:00 Milan, Tools What worked, and what to fix. One folder per job. CLAUDE.md and your voice. Scorecards. PDFs into text. Workspaces in VS Code. Your brand as a design system. This week, and session 5

/bi-session-4.h: What worked, and what to fix
/bi-session-4.t: You've each built the start of a tool already. Both examples show the same thing: the result is as good as what you put in the folder and what you write down once. Gabriel · report in Italian. A sample report did most of the work. All the documents in one folder, one past report as the example and a prompt asking it to copy the format and write in native Italian in our narrative style. The first draft got the style and the layout right and needed small edits. He asked it to double check and still found small mistakes. A general "check your work" isn't enough. The checks need writing down one by one. That's your scorecard. Alice and Riccardo · Italy and France. Reviewing went well, adding went too far. It compared the Italian documents and the French subcontractor's report and found what was missing. When Alice asked it to add some points, it wrote far more detail than we needed and Riccardo had to cut it back by hand. Next time, ask it to mark everything it adds (tracked changes or a highlight), and put a line on length in CLAUDE.md so it stays short without being told

This is how the pieces from today fit together. The case folder changes every time. The starting context and the design system stay in one place and get linked in, so you only keep one copy of each. case-folder/ one per job, named after the case CLAUDE.md read first, in every new chat sources/ the case documents: each PDF and its.md text output/ what Claude writes starting-context/ one copy on your computer, linked in the workspace INSTRUCTIONS.md the standing brief: how this job is done VOICE.md how Background Italia writes (or keep it in CLAUDE.md) SCORECARD.md the checks every draft has to pass examples/ a good past report, as text design-system/ your brand, made in the Claude app, linked the same way This follows the starter kit: INSTRUCTIONS.md, SCORECARD.md and examples/ are the files in system-template/. Don't worry about getting the layout perfect. Use it, change it and tidy it with Claude when it gets messy

Claude reads CLAUDE.md on its own before it does anything in that folder, in every new chat. You don't need to tell it to. Keep the name CLAUDE.md, and copy it into each new folder where you want the same rules. Whatever you keep correcting by hand belongs in this file. If it writes too much, have it describe a short piece of your writing and turn that description into instructions for itself. It understands its own words best, so let it write them and you approve them. Your voice can live here too, or in a VOICE.md next to it. Make it write shorter Read the short report in examples/. Describe how it's written: sentence length, how much detail, how it opens and closes. Then write instructions for yourself that make your writing as short as this, and add them to CLAUDE.md for me to approve. See what it added When you add anything to a report I've written, highlight it so I can see what's yours. Add this rule to CLAUDE.md. When results start to get worse in a long chat, start a new one. It begins again from CLAUDE.md with a clean head. Every few months, give your old.md files back to Claude and ask it to make them shorter and easier to use. The tools change, so your files should too

A scorecard is the job description you'd give a new hire, with the KPIs you'd judge them on. Gabriel called them contracts, which is close. It's as small or as big as the job needs: the more you want it to run on its own, the more exact it has to be. Simple A list in SCORECARD.md. One to ten things a good draft has. You check it yourself as you read, on the train if that's when you have time. No invented facts. Every finding has its source. Written in Italian throughout. Measured Checks with a number. For review work where a client will spot a gap. Give it a threshold it has to reach, and a way to count. Every document in sources/ is cited at least once. Every date matches its source. Assessment A table it fills in first. Before it drafts, it counts the documents, lists the key facts and flags the holes. This is what an agent runs on its own across several cases. Documents 1 to 5 are numbered in sequence. Document 4 is missing. How hard you check depends on the report too. Alice's rule from your brainstorm is a good first line: on a long report, check the key issues and findings. On a short one, check every detail, because the client accepts fewer mistakes. The best scorecards come from your own corrections. Gabriel already gives back the revised version and asks Claude to update its instructions. Do that and also say why you changed it, the way you'd brief a subcontractor. You can dictate it. Then share the file, and anyone on the team can run the job to the same standard. After you correct a draft My corrected version is in output/final.docx. Compare it with your draft. I changed it because <say why>. Update SCORECARD.md so the next draft passes these checks without me making the same changes. For more on how to think about a scorecard, use the agent scorecard tool

PDFs are messy underneath, so Claude has to guess at what's in them and can leave things out. They're also heavy, and copying them into every case folder adds up fast. Have Claude convert each one to a text (.md ) file once, then check the text against the original. The text version is what you keep in your starting context and examples. Keep the PDF only where you need the original. Convert and check Convert every PDF in sources/ to a.md file with the same name. Keep the tables as tables. Then compare each.md with its PDF and list anything missing: pages, tables, numbers, footnotes. For work that has to be complete, like litigation, put the comparison in your scorecard so it runs every time. You can also add it to CLAUDE.md: "When I add a PDF, convert it to text and check nothing was lost.". A big archive of old files costs a lot to convert this way. If you get there, ask me: there are cheaper ways to run it in the background

Gabriel was copying his starting-context folder into every new case. A workspace lets each case see that one folder without copying it. Keep starting-context/ (and later design-system/ ) in one place on your computer, outside your case folders. Open the case folder in VS Code as usual. Drag starting-context/ from File Explorer into the VS Code side panel. When it asks, choose Add Folder to Workspace so nothing gets copied. Both folders now sit in the side panel. Right-click a file, choose Copy Path and paste it into the chat when you want Claude to use it. When you close, VS Code asks to save the workspace. Say yes. It saves one small file that remembers which folders this case can see. Nothing moves on your computer. If you change a file in starting-context/, every case that links it sees the change

/bi-session-4.h: Your brand as a design system
/bi-session-4.t: The same idea as the PDFs, for how things look. Give Claude your brand guidelines, presentations, Word files, PDFs or your website. It turns them into a design system: small, exact files for your logo, colours, fonts and spacing. What it's for. Reports and proposals that look the same every time. Layout rules you'd otherwise fix by hand, like "a table never splits across two pages". A separate version where Italy and France look different. LinkedIn posts in your style, built from your old posts. Where to find it. You make it in the Claude desktop app or at claude.ai. It isn't part of VS Code. Claude Design has moved into Artifacts, which is why Alice couldn't find it. The old claude.ai/design closes on 14 December 2026. Download the folder and link it into your workspace like starting-context/. Any web designer could use it, and so can Mistral or another AI. The setup guide takes about 15 minutes and works on your Pro plan: Create a design system in Claude. There's a version for your AI too, if you'd rather it walked you through. Alice, I'll call you for 10 minutes this week to set it up for the team

Everyone: write a scorecard for one of your jobs, with a number wherever you can count something. Use your instructions on one real job and note what you still had to correct. Who This week Bring on 11 November Alice. Add the "write shorter" and "highlight what you add" rules to CLAUDE.md. Set up the design system with me. A proposal and the report that came from it. Gabriel. Convert the PDFs in your starting context to text and run the check. Move starting-context/ out of your case folders and link it in a workspace. Your litigation and directorship chart, with its scorecard. Riccardo. Try your next translation from one folder with a CLAUDE.md. A translation: the source and your final version. Manuela. Collect three or four posts you'd like it to write like. Your LinkedIn and social media examples. Veronica. Try your next translation or interview report the same way. A translation or an interview report, before and after. Redacted, dummy or public material only, as always. Session 5: Tools. Next week I'll show you my own setup and a reference guide to everything my system is connected to, past Gmail, Google Drive and the browser, including a few small Python scripts. Then we look at what we can connect to your accounts properly. Also bring: Your template The report, proposal or chart layout you fill in by hand. Your copy and paste The files you copy from every week, and where they live. What you corrected Your notes from this week's real job. Stuck on any of this? Reply to any of my emails and we'll do a short call before Wednesday

/bi-specialist-tools.t: Praxis programme · Handout · Specialist tools. Which AI for which specialist job Claude stays your everyday tool. For a few jobs another tool does better, and this is the short list, built around what you've brought me: the Vinted profile picture, the photo of rocks and sea and the documents that need to stay in Europe. After our call on Fri 13 November 2026 Next: Wed 2 December, 11:00 to 12:00 Milan, Tools The short version. Find where a picture appears. Where was this photo taken. Faces: check before you search. Text out of scans and images. Cloud, Europe or your own machine. Try it before 2 December

Each of the big AI companies trained its models on different material and is better at different things. You don't need a subscription to all of them. Most of what's below is free, or works on a free account. Reports, translation, your folders. Claude in VS Code It works with your files, your CLAUDE.md and your scorecards. Where else a picture appears. Google Lens Yandex Bing TinEye One engine finding nothing proves nothing. Use all four. Where a photo was taken. ChatGPT Gemini Picarta They guess with confidence. A guess is a lead to check, never a finding. Scans, tables, text in images. Mistral Gemini Check the text against the original, as with your PDFs. Images for a proposal or a post. ChatGPT Gemini Never make images of real people or anything that could pass as evidence. Sensitive documents kept in Europe. Mistral Needs more setup than Claude. I'm packaging that for you. Personal data you can't send anywhere. A model on your own computer Needs its own machine. My proposal follows. Specialist geolocation, for firms. Raven (the old GeoSpy) For vetted companies, hundreds a month. Only if it becomes a weekly job

Alice's everyday case: a profile picture on a selling platform like Vinted, and you want to know where else it's been used. You already use Google Lens in Chrome. Add three more engines and you'll find a lot more, because each one has its own index. Save it at full size Right-click, save. No screenshot Google Lens crop one thing at a time Yandex strong on faces, Eastern Europe Bing social media copies TinEye sort by oldest Log each hit link and date found, like any source Google Lens. In Chrome, right-click the picture and choose Search with Google. Drag the box to crop to the face, then the background, then an object. Each crop gives you different results. Yandex and Bing. Upload the same file at yandex.com/images and bing.com/visualsearch. TinEye. At tineye.com, sort the results by Oldest. The first time a picture appeared online is often the most useful thing you'll find: a stock photo, a stolen picture or the person's first account. Photos on Vinted, Instagram or Facebook usually have their hidden details (camera, date, GPS) removed. A photo a client sends you as an original file may still have them. Check it on your own computer, so the file stays with you. On a Mac, open it in Preview and choose Tools, Show Inspector. On Windows, right-click the file, Properties, Details

Riccardo's case: a picture of rocks and sea, and the question of where it is. Use the AI for the leads and a map for the proof. AI for the leads The map for the proof Ask two AIs ChatGPT and Gemini, separately 3 candidates each with its clues Google Earth 3D coastline, rocks Street View, Mapillary from the ground SunCalc shadows, time of day PeakVisor skyline Proof in the report photo and map side by side Where the two AIs agree, start there. Where they don't, you have more places to check. The AI's guess never goes in the report. The side-by-side with the matching features marked does. Prompt for ChatGPT and Gemini Where could this photo have been taken? First list every clue you can see: rock type, plants, colour of the water, the light and the sun, buildings, boats, anything written. Then give me your three best guesses, each with the clues that support it and how sure you are. I need places to check, so don't give me just one answer. When you have a candidate I think this photo was taken at <place>. What should I look for in Google Earth or Street View to confirm it or rule it out? List the features in the photo that should match. Use ChatGPT with thinking switched on. The AI tools sometimes refuse to locate a photo of a private person or their home. Upload only pictures you're allowed to share with that company, and check the training setting on any account you use for work

There are search engines that look for a face rather than a picture, such as PimEyes and FaceCheck.ID. They work, and in Italy they're a legal risk for you. Picture search. Finds copies of that one picture. Use it freely, within your AI policy. Face search. Finds the person in other photos. That's biometric data, a special category under GDPR. The Garante fined Clearview AI €20 million in 2022 for collecting faces of people in Italy. Before anyone on the team uses a face search, agree when it's allowed, on what legal basis and who signs it off, and add that to your AI policy from session 1

/bi-specialist-tools.h: Text out of scans and images
/bi-specialist-tools.t: The same idea as your PDFs in session 4. Get the text out once, check it against the original, then work from the text. The scan stamps, tables, handwriting Mistral or Gemini Claude is fine for clean scans A.md file [unreadable] where it's unsure Check it against the original Scan into text Turn this scan into text. Keep the layout and the tables. Where you can't read a word or a number, write [unreadable] instead of guessing. At the end, list every place you weren't sure

/bi-specialist-tools.h: Cloud, Europe or your own machine
/bi-specialist-tools.t: Three levels, for three kinds of work. Decide which level a job needs before you start it, the same way you'd decide who on the team should see a file. Everyday: Claude. Reports, proposals, translation, your instructions and scorecards. Most of your work stays here. Redacted case files, public sources, your templates. Stays in Europe: Mistral. A specialist that only reads the sensitive documents. You build the system with Claude. For a client who wants their data processed in the EU. Never leaves the office: a machine of your own. For Alice's list of former employees, it works like this: The sensitive list names, addresses Office machine names out, codes in, no internet Clean version no one can be identified Claude the analysis and the chart The key that turns the codes back into names stays on the office machine. Mistral is on hold until I send the setup package, so pausing the subscription until January is the right call. The proposal for the machine follows separately

Everyone: take one picture from a closed or public case and run it through the picture search or the location steps. Write down which tool found something first and what you had to check by hand. Your picture A closed or public case only, as always. What each tool found Google, Yandex, Bing, TinEye, ChatGPT or Gemini. How you confirmed it Or where you got stuck. Found a specialist tool I haven't listed, or a job you'd like a tool for? Send it to me and I'll add it here

/bi-team-files.t: Praxis programme · Handout · Team files. One set of files the whole team uses Each of you has started your own instructions and scorecards. Now we put the ones that work in one place, so anyone can run a job to the same standard, and nothing is lost when someone leaves. After our call on Fri 13 November 2026 We set it up together: Wed 2 December, 11:00 Milan One team library. Point to it, don't copy it. Keep it up to date. Before Riccardo's last day

Put a folder called team-library on the shared drive you already use (Google Drive or SharePoint) and sync it to everyone's computer. It holds how you do the work. Client documents stay in the case folder. Case A client documents Case B client documents Case C client documents team-library instructions, scorecards, voice, redacted examples The case folders point to the library. The library never holds client documents. team-library/ README.md what's here and who looks after each job VOICE.md how Background Italia writes, in Italian and English design-system/ your brand, from the Claude app jobs/ dd-report-review/ one folder per job you repeat INSTRUCTIONS.md the standing brief SCORECARD.md the checks every draft has to pass LOG.md what changed, when and why examples/ a good past report as text, redacted translation/ registry-chart/ media-screening/ interview-report/ The job folders are the system-template/ from your starter kit, one copy per job. Each job has one owner who looks after its files. Anyone can use them

/bi-team-files.h: Point to it, don't copy it
/bi-team-files.t: When you copy the files into each case, you end up with ten versions and nobody knows which is right. Copy into every case. v1 v2 v2b final? A fix made in one case never reaches the others. Point to the library. one Fix it once and every case gets the fix. There are two ways to point. Use the first, and the second if you'd rather not open a workspace each time. Add it to your workspace. Open the case folder in VS Code, drag team-library into the side panel and choose Add Folder to Workspace. Save the workspace when you close. The workspaces guide has a screenshot for every step. One line in CLAUDE.md. In the case folder's CLAUDE.md, write @ and the full path to the library file. Claude reads it every time, as if it were in the folder. Get the path with right-click, Copy Path, because it's different on each computer. A case CLAUDE.md that points to the library This case is a due diligence report review. Follow @/Users/alice/Google Drive/team-library/jobs/dd-report-review/INSTRUCTIONS.md Check every draft against @/Users/alice/Google Drive/team-library/jobs/dd-report-review/SCORECARD.md Write the way @/Users/alice/Google Drive/team-library/VOICE.md describes. The first time, Claude asks whether it may read files from outside the folder. Say yes. Don't use a Mac alias or a Windows shortcut. Claude sees it as a small file of its own and can't see inside the folder it points to. That's the most likely reason it didn't work when Alice and Gabriel tried

The files only get better if your corrections go back into them. Alice's subcontractor report is the example: she made the last small changes in the final report, and now they need to go into the instructions so the next report has them too. The owner makes the changes. Anyone else adds a note to LOG.md or tells the owner. Watch for conflict copies. Two people editing the same file at once on a shared drive makes a second copy. Give both to Claude and ask it to merge them. Tidy every couple of months. Ask Claude to make the files shorter and easier to read. Tools change, so your files should too. After you change the final version by hand My final version is <paste the path>. Compare it with your draft and list what I changed. Then update INSTRUCTIONS.md in the team library so the next draft has these changes without me making them. Add a line to LOG.md with today's date, what changed and why

Riccardo has built instructions and prompts that work: his Italy and Hong Kong media report had the right voice and depth. They go into the library before he leaves, so the team keeps them. This week Make the team-library folder. Thu 19 Nov Riccardo's files in the library. Wed 2 Dec We link it into one real case together. January Every job runs from the library. For Riccardo, in each folder he's worked in List every instructions file, prompt, scorecard and example I've made in this folder. For the ones another person could use, copy them into team-library/jobs/<job name>/ and write a short README.md: what the job is, how to start it and what to watch out for. Leave out anything with client names or personal details. On 2 December, bring the files you use most

/claude-privacy.t: Privacy guide Stop Claude training on your chats On a personal Claude plan, Anthropic asks whether it can use your chats and coding sessions to train its models. One switch in Settings turns that off, in the desktop app, on claude.ai and in Claude Code. Updated. November 2026 Time needed. About 2 minutes Applies to. Free, Pro and Max plans Step 01

With the switch on, what you type into Claude can end up in the data Anthropic trains its next models on, and Anthropic keeps those chats for up to 5 years. With it off, they're kept for 30 days and stay out of training. That matters as soon as you work with real material: a client's figures, a candidate's CV, a draft contract, the files Claude Code reads in your VS Code folder. The setting covers your chats and your coding sessions, so the one switch also covers Claude Code when you're signed in with the same account (see the VS Code setup guide). On a Team or Enterprise plan, or using Claude through the API? Those run under Anthropic's commercial terms, and your chats aren't used for training. You may not see this switch at all. If in doubt, ask whoever manages your company's Claude account. Step 02

Open the Claude app and click your name in the bottom-left corner. 1 Fig. 1 The Claude app home screen. 1 Your name and plan. Click it to open the account menu. 1 2 Fig. 2 The account menu. 1 The account you're signed in to. If you have more than one Claude account, check it's the one you work in and repeat these steps for each of the others. 2 Settings. Shortcut ⌘, / Ctrl+,. Step 03

/claude-privacy.h: Switch off Help improve our AI models
/claude-privacy.t: In Settings, click Privacy in the list on the left. The switch is under Preferences. 1 2 Fig. 3 Settings, Privacy. Here the switch is already off. 1 Privacy, in the Settings list. 2 Help improve our AI models. Click the switch so it turns grey with the knob on the left. Blue with the knob on the right means it's still on. The change saves straight away, so you can close Settings. It follows your account, which means it applies on claude.ai, in the phone app and in Claude Code too. Location metadata sits just above. It lets Claude use your rough location (city or region) to tailor answers. It has nothing to do with training, so leave it on or off as you prefer. Step 04

/claude-privacy.h: What the switch does and doesn't cover

When the time comes, Claude starts a fresh chat on its own, does the work and saves the result under Scheduled in the left sidebar. It can search the web, read the files and connected apps you've given it access to (your calendar, email, Drive and so on) and make a document or a page. Good jobs for it are the ones that start with "go and look at.": checking for new regulations, a morning brief from your calendar and inbox, a weekly summary of what changed in a shared file, a reminder list for Friday. Most tasks run on Anthropic's servers, so they run on time even when your laptop is asleep or the app is closed. Tasks that need your computer are different. /evals.t: Praxis · Is the work good? Evals: proving the output is good A script can give you the same output every time and still be wrong every time. It can drop the VAT column on every run, reliably, forever. An eval is how you find out whether the work is right, and it's what lets you change your rules without fear. Takes about 15 minutes to read, 30 to try Before this Writing your skill file

An eval is a test for work that has no single correct answer. It has three parts: Test cases: inputs you've chosen on purpose, including the awkward ones. The thing you're testing: your skill file and your script, as they stand today. A grader: something that decides whether each output passed. Anthropic's own prompt evaluations course teaches the same three parts, then splits on the last one: who grades. A person, a piece of code or another model. For our purposes there are two families. Human evals, where a person reads the output against a written rubric, are slow and expensive and still the gold standard, because a person catches the thing you never thought to check. Machine evals, where code or a model grades it, are fast and repeatable and run on every change, but you have to decide in advance what "right" means. You need both. Human evals tell you what to measure, and machine evals measure it for you from then on

Take the BD analyst from the skill file guide, the one writing prospect research memos. The skill file says lead with the decision, cite every factual claim and keep the executive summary to 3 sentences. A human eval for that is a rubric and a stack of outputs. The rubric has one row per rule, worded so two people would grade it the same way: # Criterion Pass when 1. Decision first. The first sentence is a recommendation, with no background before it. 2. Citations. Every factual claim has (Source: file, p.N). 3. Citations hold up. Spot-check 3 citations: the page says what the memo says it says. 4. Summary length. The executive summary is 3 sentences or fewer. 5. Leadership flag. A leadership change in the last 18 months is flagged, or there wasn't one. 6. Client vocabulary. Industry terms match the client's own words. 7. Would I send it. Would you put your name on this as it is? Number 7 catches everything the first six missed. When it fails while 1 to 6 pass, you've found a rule that isn't in your skill file yet, and finding those is the point of the exercise. Be strict about how you grade: Grade 20 outputs. Three tells you nothing, 20 is enough to see a pattern. Grade blind. Hide which version produced which output, or you'll mark your own improvements generously. Use two graders working separately, then compare. Where two careful people disagree, the rubric's wording is unclear, so fix it before you grade anything else. Write each failure down word for word: the actual sentence and what was wrong with it. Those notes are what you use to write the next version of your skill file. Keep a log, one entry per run, in the folder next to the skill file: 2026-07-14 | skill.md v4 | 20 memos | graders: DM, RK Score: 17/20 pass on all criteria Failures: - 3 memos led with company background instead of the recommendation (crit 1) - 1 memo cited a page number that didn't contain the claim (crit 3) - 2 memos used "vessel" where the client says "rig" (crit 6) Disagreement between graders: 2 of 140 judgements (both on crit 7) Action: rule 1 rewritten to "First sentence must contain the word 'recommend' or 'do not recommend'." Re-run next week. That log is worth more than the score. It shows how your rules got tighter over time, and why

A machine eval is a script that grades the output of your script. It comes in two kinds. Graded by code, when the answer can be checked. For pulling data out of documents, sorting things into categories, formatting or anything else with a factually correct answer, you don't need judgement. You need a comparison. So you build a golden set: a handful of inputs where you've written down the right answer by hand. Here's one we built for an invoice script: six invoices, an expected.csv with the right answer for each and a check.py that compares them. Running python3 evals/check.py prints: GOLDEN SET PASS 001-clean.txt PASS 002-missing-po.txt PASS 003-no-vat-line.txt PASS 004-multiline-address.txt FAIL 005-duplicate-date.txt date: expected '2026-04-21' but got '2026-05-21' PASS 006-rounding-mismatch.txt RULE CHECKS PASS columns match skill.md rule 1 (order and names) PASS currency codes are all in the allowed set FAIL net + vat == gross for every row 006-rounding-mismatch.txt: 1099.99 + 220.00!= 1320.00 PASS no field invented where the source was silent DETERMINISM PASS two consecutive runs produced the same content hash 9 passed, 2 failed Both failures are real, and they fail in different ways. 005-duplicate-date has two lines labelled Date:, an invoice date and a payment due date. The script takes the last one and the right answer is the first. That's a bug in the script and a gap in the skill file, which never said which date wins, so the fix goes in both. The arithmetic check catches something else. 006-rounding-mismatch doesn't add up because the invoice itself is wrong: the script copied it faithfully. That failure should stay on screen until a person has looked at the document. An eval that flags bad source data is doing the job of the senior person who used to notice. The golden set cases aren't random. 002-missing-po is there because a rule says a missing field becomes an empty cell. 005-duplicate-date is there because a real invoice had two date lines and nobody had decided which one counts. Every case is a bug that happened or a rule that turned out to be unclear, and the set grows one incident at a time. The rule checks don't need a right answer at all. They're things that must hold for any input: the columns are the ones the skill file lists, currencies come from a known list, net plus VAT equals gross and nothing appears in the output that wasn't in the source. They're quick to write and each one catches a whole family of mistakes, so start here if

Look at the output before you build anything. Take 20 real outputs, read them and write down every failure in plain words. Hamel Husain, who builds evals for clients, puts this reading at 60 to 80% of the time on a real project. The graders are the easy part. Knowing what to grade is the hard part. Then sort the failures into two piles. Each one that keeps coming back is either a missing rule, which goes in the skill file, or a check you should have had, which goes in the eval. Every incident lands somewhere, so nothing depends on someone remembering. Start with 10 to 20 cases. Anthropic's advice for writing skills is to create at least 3 evals before you write long instructions, and to measure how the model does without your skill file first, so you can tell whether your rules helped. Go for volume over polish. Anthropic's own eval principles say more cases with slightly rougher automatic grading beat a few perfect ones graded by hand. Fifty rough automatic checks beat five perfect manual ones. Run the evals on every change: every skill file edit, every script change, every model upgrade. That's what pays for the whole exercise, because it tells you when a change that fixed one thing broke another. Without it you're editing rules and hoping. And keep the log: date, version, sample size, score, failures and what you changed

/evals.h: Why it matters more for you than for a developer
/evals.t: A developer who ships a bug ships a fix. You sign your name to the output. If you're putting a memo in front of a client, a filing in front of a regulator or a recommendation in front of a partner, "the AI seemed good" won't stand up. An eval gives you something that will: here are the criteria, here's the sample, here's the score, here's what failed and what we changed. It's the standard you already apply to a junior's work, written down. It lets you change the rules. Editing a skill file that works is nerve-racking when you might break something you can't see. With an eval you edit, run it and know within a minute. Fear of breaking things is what keeps these systems stuck at version one. It catches drift. The model underneath gets upgraded, your documents change format, a case turns up that nobody expected. None of that announces itself, and the eval catches it on the next run. And it's an asset you keep. Your golden set and your rubric are your professional standards, written down and checkable by a machine. The skill file says what good looks like and the eval proves you got there, and neither one lives in anyone's head any more

/evals.h: Try it this week, in 30 minutes
/evals.t: Take 10 real inputs you've already processed. For each one, write down the right answer by hand: a row in a CSV, or two lines on what a good output must contain. That's your golden set. It's the slow part, and you only do it once. Ask Claude Code to write a check.py like the one above that compares your outputs with your golden set and checks the rules in your skill file. Run it and count the failures. Fix the most common failure, in the skill file rather than the script. Run it again and write the log entry. You now have rules, proof they run the same way twice and proof they give the right answer. That's a system you can hand to somebody else

/hsa-session-4.h: Where Claude looks for your rules

A skill you make in the app can show up in VS Code when you're signed in to the same account (type /skills to see which ones). To be sure, keep a copy in your personal.claude folder. This is where we go next week. Claude in VS Code. works on the folder you open You, in every folder.claude in your user folder How you like answers: short, English (South Africa), ask before guessing. Only you see it. All HSA work HSA\CLAUDE.md The house rules: the HSA format, trusted sources, NQF 4, no learner data. Shared with the team. Question bank CLAUDE.md Moodle format, 3 per criterion. /hsa-session-4.h: CLAUDE.md is the one Claude reads by itself
/hsa-session-4.t: I mentioned a voice.md alongside CLAUDE.md. The difference matters: CLAUDE.md is the only file Claude reads at the start of every chat. That's what Laetitia's Claude did this morning: it kept CLAUDE.md short and pointed to the HSA format instead of copying every rule in. That's the right way round. There are two ways to point. Paste into Claude in your HSA folder Make a CLAUDE.md for this folder from what we've agreed so far. Keep it under 40 lines. /hsa-session-4.h: A request in CLAUDE.md, a rule in settings
/hsa-session-4.t: When I talked about blocking websites, the block sits in a settings file. Claude reads CLAUDE.md and tries to follow it. Settings are rules the program enforces, so Claude can't talk its way round them. In CLAUDE.md. "Use official sources and tell me when you do.". Flexible. Claude can still settle a contradiction, like it did for Elsa. It's a request. In a long chat Claude can drift, as Laetitia found. In.claude\settings.json. Claude has to ask you before every search, or can't search at all. Enforced every time, in that folder only. "Ask" is the middle ground Elsa wanted: you see each source and say yes or no. Change it back when you do want open research in that folder. What the file says (ask first) { "permissions": { "ask": ["WebSearch", "WebFetch"] } } You don't need to type it. /hsa-session-4.h: Sharing your rules with each other
/hsa-session-4.t: Not everyone can reach the same OneDrive, so you chose a Teams channel. That's a good place to start. A Teams channel, now. Everyone can reach it today. Put the HSA folder (with its.claude folder) in the channel's Files. Each of you copies it to your laptop and opens it in VS Code. Copies drift. Agree one owner per file and post in the channel when you change it. A private GitHub repository, later. When several of you edit the same rules. Every change saved with who, when and why. Go back to any version, and merge two people's work. Claude does the saving and describes the changes, so you don't learn commands. A new account, which IT may want to approve first

Start a new chat for each new piece of work. It's like starting the day after a good night's sleep. The chat forgets the last conversation and goes back to your CLAUDE.md. Elsa noticed it still remembers some things: those come from the files in the folder and Claude's own notes, which is the point. Put a reminder in your calendar for two or three months from now. /hsa-session-5.h: Artifacts: work you can open and share
/hsa-session-5.t: An artifact is a page Claude builds next to the chat: a chart, a table, a calendar or a small tool. It opens in its own panel, you can keep changing it in the chat, and you can share it as a link. Use the word "artifact" in your request and Claude knows what you mean. 1 · The risk register for the board. 20 min Christine drives You already have Claude pulling the register apart and drawing graphs. As an artifact it becomes one page: what's most likely and most serious, who owns it and what happens next. Prompt 1 Attached is our risk register. Make an artifact for the board: - a heat map of likelihood against impact, with each risk as a numbered dot - the 5 highest risks with owner, next action and due date - what changed since the last version, if the file shows it Use only what is in the file. Risk register · example only Artifact 4 3 1 3 4 2 2 6 5 1 Impact, low to high 1 Venues fully booked in peak months. 2 New curriculum not approved in time. 3 Moodle move runs late. 4 Key author unavailable. 5 Learners share test questions. /sandbox-to-live.t: Praxis programme · Handout · Building safely. From your sandbox to something customers use Your team can build its own tools now. The worry we hear in every company is how to do that without breaking the systems everyone already relies on. The answer is to build in one place and use in another, with someone who checks each tool before it moves across. For any team building its own tools About 5 minutes to read The four places a tool lives. The words we use, and IT's words. What happens in each place. The check before anything goes live. Step by step, from idea to live. What we set up with you

/sandbox-to-live.h: The four places a tool lives
/sandbox-to-live.t: Two places to build and try things, then one check and the live system. A tool only ever moves left to right. Building and trying In use My sandbox your own computer, only you Team sandbox shared, inside the organisation The check signed off by IT, or by us Live customers, colleagues, real work A change to a live tool goes back to the team sandbox and through the check again. Nobody edits the live version directly

/sandbox-to-live.h: The words we use, and IT's words
/sandbox-to-live.t: Engineers say development and production. Most of the people building tools now aren't engineers, so we use plain names. Keep this table for when you talk to IT or a supplier. We say IT says What it means My sandbox. Local development. Folders on your computer where you try things with Claude. Only you see it. Team sandbox. Development or staging server. A shared copy the whole team can open, use and test. It sits inside the company, behind a login. The check. Review, QA, release approval. Someone who didn't build the tool looks at it and signs it off. Live. Production. The version customers and colleagues rely on every day, with real information in it

The further right, the more people depend on it, so the more care it gets. My sandbox Team sandbox Live Who uses it. You. Your team, each with their own login. Customers and colleagues. What's in it. Samples and the documents you're allowed to use. Real documents can be used, and they stay inside the organisation. Nothing is public. Real customers, real workflows, real information. If it breaks. You start again and nobody notices. The team waits while it's fixed. Customers notice. Where the work is kept. A folder on your computer. A GitHub repository in your organisation's account. The signed-off version from that same repository. Who looks after it. You. The team, with one named owner per tool. Your IT team, or us until you have one. Where the team sandbox runs. As soon as a tool is for more than one person, it needs somewhere shared to run. Two ways to do it, and the code lives in your GitHub organisation either way. A private server online. A server rented in Europe, only reachable with your team's logins. Paid monthly. Works from home, other offices and on the road. Nothing to buy, easy to grow. Your documents sit with a hosting company, so it goes in your data records. A machine in the office. A box such as an NVIDIA DGX Spark or a Mac Studio, on your own network. It can run AI models itself. Bought once. Sensitive documents never leave the building. The whole team shares one machine. Hardware to buy and a cupboard to lock

/sandbox-to-live.h: The check before anything goes live
/sandbox-to-live.t: Five questions. A tool goes live when all five have a yes and someone has signed for it. Data. What does it read, where does that go and who can see it? Does it match your AI charter? Security. Logins for each person, no passwords or keys inside the code, and only the right people can change it. Connections. If it touches an older system (accounts, stock, the CRM), it has been tested on a copy first and it reads before it ever writes. It does the job. It passes its scorecard on real examples, checked by the people who'll use it. An owner and a way back. One named person looks after it, and if something goes wrong we can switch back to the last good version in minutes. Who signs it off. You have an IT team. Your IT team signs. We prepare the sign-off pack with the team (what the tool does, the five answers, the test results) so IT can review it quickly and say yes or ask for changes. You don't. I sign, with a specialist where needed. I take responsibility for the sign-off. When a tool needs more than I can check, I bring in a specialist in security or data protection, or someone who knows your older systems inside out. The person who signs is never someone who built the tool. They come to it fresh from outside the team and check what it does with real information before your customers see it

/sandbox-to-live.h: Step by step, from idea to live
/sandbox-to-live.t: Step 1 is what we already do in the programme. Steps 2 to 6 are where you need a hand, and each one is a separate piece of work we quote for. 1 Build in your own sandbox. Your folders, your rules file and Claude on your computer. You try things and nothing else is touched. In the programme. 2 Set up the team sandbox. Your GitHub organisation, the shared server or office machine, a login for each person and the rules for what data goes in. Set-up, quoted once. 3 Build and test together. Everyone works on the same repository. The people who'll use the tool try it on real examples and score it. Your team, with support. 4 The check. The sign-off pack, the five questions, a specialist if the tool needs one, and a signature. Quoted per tool. 5 Go live. The signed-off version moves across. We tell the people using it what changed and watch the first week closely. Part of the check. 6 Look after it. Every change goes back to step 3. A short monthly look at what's live: who uses it, what broke, what's next. Monthly, if you want it

/sandbox-to-live.h: What we set up with you
/sandbox-to-live.t: Building on laptops is where every team starts, and it works for one person. The moment a tool is shared, it needs a proper home. Shared without a team sandbox. The tool runs on one laptop and stops when that person is away. Copies get emailed round and nobody knows which one is right. A quick fix goes straight to the people using it. IT finds out last and says no. With a team sandbox and a check. Everyone uses the same version, from wherever they work. Every change has a name, a reason and a way back. Testing happens where customers can't see it. IT gets a pack they can say yes to. Team sandbox set-up. We choose the server or office machine with you, set up your GitHub organisation, logins and data rules, then move your first tool in. Quoted once. The check and going live. The sign-off pack, the review against the five questions, the signature, the move to live and the first week after. Quoted per tool. Specialists when you need them. Security or data protection, or someone who knows your accounting, stock or CRM system. I find them, brief them and stay in the loop. Quoted when needed. Looking after it. A monthly look at what's live, changes taken back through the check, and someone to call when it misbehaves. Monthly. The first step: pick the one tool your team most wants to share. We look at it together for an hour, and I come back with a quote for the team sandbox and its first sign-off

/session-2.t: Praxis programme · Session 2. Define good Before you hand a job to AI, you need to know what a good result looks like.
