"Summarise the Q3 accounts" makes Claude guess which file you mean. Name the file and it reads that one, and it can tell you which page each number came from. Here's the folder we use all session. A real session. The message names the file, praxis-agent-scorecard.md, and Claude's first step is to read that file and nothing else. Then it goes on to build the handout. Right-click any file. Add File to Chat puts it straight into the Claude box. Copy Path or Copy Relative Path gives you the name to paste into your message. fenwick-rowe/CLAUDE.md # Fenwick & Rowe: client work - Before you make any document, read brand/BRAND.md and follow it. - Every number says the file and page it came from. - Can't find it? Write [NOT IN SOURCE]. - Not sure? Write [CHECK]. - Save finished files in output/. Never write over a file in sources/. - Write like our past letters in brand/examples. The rules file in our example folder, next to brand/, sources/, templates/ and output/. Copy it into your own folder and change the names. Type @ and the file name Start typing @q3 in the Claude box and pick the file from the list. Works for folders too: @sources/. Send the open file With a file open in the editor, press Option K on a Mac or Alt K on Windows. Select some lines first and it sends just those, with their line numbers. Copy the path Right-click any file in the Explorer, choose Copy Relative Path and paste it into your message. The CLAUDE.md file is read at the start of every conversation in that folder, so the rules above apply to every job without you typing them again. When Claude asks to run a script, read what it says it will do, then say yes

A design system sounds grand. For us it's one file, brand/BRAND.md, that says what your documents look like and how you write. Claude builds it from documents you already have, and every PDF, sheet and chart after that comes out in your colours. What goes in BRAND.md Fenwick & Rowe's, short enough to read in a minute. Colours #1F4D45 main #B8862F highlight #F6F3EC paper #B9BFBB past data Fonts Fraunces for headings, Inter for text. If they're missing, Georgia and Arial. Logo brand/logo.svg, top left, never stretched, white on green. Layout A4, 20 mm margins, page number and "Confidential" in the footer. Charts Past periods in grey, the period that matters in green, one brass highlight at most. Voice British spelling, short sentences, "we" for the firm. Look at brand/examples for how we write. Fenwick & Rowe Q3 client summary · Confidential Q3 at a glance. Revenue up on Q2, margin steady and cash enough for 4 months of costs. Revenue €412,300 Accounts p. 2 Gross margin 38.4% Accounts p. 3 Debtor days [NOT IN SOURCE] Ask the client Made by Claude from brand/BRAND.md and sources/q3-accounts.pdf. The firm and figures are examples. Build your brand file Look at the documents in @brand/examples/ and write brand/BRAND.md: our colours as hex codes, fonts, where the logo goes, page layout, how charts should look and how we write. Ask me about anything you can't tell from the files

/session-2.h: Three files, and what good looks like
/session-2.t: Claude can read and make PDFs, Excel workbooks and Word documents. A file that opens isn't the same as a file you'd send. Here's what we check before it goes anywhere. Fenwick & Rowe Q3 summary Q3 at a glance €412k p. 2 38.4% p. 3 €96k p. 5 Debtor days [NOT IN SOURCE] Read a PDF, make a PDF.pdf. Read @sources/q3-accounts.pdf. Give me revenue, margin and cash, each with its page number. Then make a one-page summary following @brand/BRAND.md. Good looks like. Every number has a page, and the page says that number. Anything missing says [NOT IN SOURCE]. Fits on one page, logo and colours from the brand file. Watch for. Numbers rounded differently from the accounts. Text cut off at the bottom of the page. fx =SUM(B2:B4). Month Revenue Costs 2. July. 131,900. 82,400. 3. August. 126,050. 79,100. 4. September. 154,350. 92,500. 5. Q3. 412,300. 254,000. Summary July Aug Sep Notes Build a workbook.xlsx. Turn @sources/q3-transactions.csv into a workbook: a tab per month, a summary tab with formulas, headers in our brand green. Good looks like. Click a total and you see a formula like =SUM, so it updates when a number changes. Q3 total matches the accounts: €412,300. A Notes tab says where the data came from. Watch for. Totals typed in as plain numbers. #REF! or #VALUE! anywhere in the sheet. Your Q3 results Claude Debtor days not in the accounts. Ask before sending? Draft in your template.docx. Draft the Q3 client letter in @templates/client-letter.docx using the summary. Keep our styles. Put anything you're unsure of in a comment. Good looks like. Headings use the template's styles, so the contents page and spacing still work. Reads like your past letters, no AI phrasing. Doubts sit in comments, out of the text. Watch for. "I hope this finds you well" and friends. Bold and font sizes typed in by hand. To make Excel and Word files, Claude writes a short script and asks to run it. The file lands in output/, and you open it in Excel or Word as normal. Open every file before you trust it

Same data, same request, one with the brand file and a clear brief. This is the example we use for "what good looks like": hours spent on the monthly client report, before and after the brief and scorecard went in. First try "Make a chart of the report hours" With the brief Brand file, plus five rules Title says what happened "Report time down from 6.5 to 2.2 hours", where the first try said "Chart 1". Colours mean something Grey for before, green for after. Six colours made you read a legend. Values on the bars Nobody has to read numbers off an axis. Starts at zero The first try started at 2, so June's bar looked 24 times shorter than March's. The real gap is about 3 times. Says where it's from A source line, so anyone can check it. The brief behind the good chart Make a bar chart of report hours by month from @output/run-log.xlsx. Follow @brand/BRAND.md. Title it with what the data shows, put the value on each bar, start the axis at zero and add a source line underneath. Save it as a PNG in output/

Everything we checked today becomes a scorecard: the standard every piece of AI work on that job gets judged against. Here's Fenwick & Rowe's for the monthly client summary. Each check is something a colleague could tick without asking you. # Check How you test it Pass when 1. No invented facts. Open 3 cited pages and find the number. All 3 match. 2. Complete. Compare with last month's summary. Every section there, gaps marked [NOT IN SOURCE]. 3. Totals add up. Click the totals in the workbook. Formulas, and they match the accounts. 4. On brand. Put it next to a past report. Same colours, fonts and logo position. 5. Sounds like us. Read the first paragraph aloud. You'd send it without rewording. "No invented facts" is always check number one. Four out of five is a fail: fix the brief or the brand file, then run it again. Build your own with the agent scorecard tool

About an hour, on your own machine. Use redacted or dummy files until your AI policy is agreed. Set up the folder Make brand/, sources/, templates/ and output/. Copy the CLAUDE.md rules from this page. Build your brand file Put three of your own documents in brand/examples and run the brand prompt above. Make one real file Pick the task from session 1. Point Claude at the source with @ and ask for a PDF, a workbook or a Word draft. Score it Write 5 checks in the scorecard tool. Score Claude's file, then one of your own recent pieces of work. Start your scorecard I do this job every [week / month]: [describe it]. Here's a good example I made: @[file]. Help me write 5 checks for a good result. Each check needs a way to test it and a clear pass. "No invented facts" is check 1. Bring to session 3: the file Claude made, your scorecard with both scores, and one thing you'd change in the brief. If it only half worked, bring that too: it's the most useful thing to look at together. Stuck on setup? Reply to any of our emails and we'll book a short one-to-one before the next session

/session-3.t: Praxis programme · Session 3. Which tool, and what to hand over In session 3 you drive. You show us what you tried with the starter kit, even if it only half worked, because that's the most useful thing to see. Here's the hour and what we covered, to keep. You leave with a scorecard for your first system, and a view on which tool works for you

Most of it is on your screens. 5 min Where we are. Everyone starts from a different place. That's expected. 30 min Show and tell. About six minutes each. Share your screen and walk us through it. 17 min Run your starter kit. Everyone at once, in their own folder. It writes your scorecard with you. 8 min Which tool, and next week. What worked for you, and what to bring to session 4

Show it rather than describe it. If you got stuck, show us where you stopped. What did you do? Which folder, which AI, which task. How did you do it? What you typed, and what it gave back. What aren't you sure about? Anything. There are no silly questions here. Open your starter kit folder and type Read CLAUDE.md and let's start. I'm <your name>. It asks about your task, then agrees with you what a good result looks like. Redacted or dummy files only

/session-3.h: How we know the work is good
/session-3.t: The AI writes the draft. Your scorecard decides whether it's good enough, and a person signs it off. When it fails, we fix the instructions, so the next run is better too. An example scorecard, one run Extracting directorships from three registry PDFs into a table. 1 No invented facts Every name, date and share is on the page it cites Pass 2 Complete All three PDFs read, and the row count matches what you'd expect Pass 3 Correct data Five rows picked at random, checked against the source Fail 4 Right format Matches the table the client is used to Pass 5 Sounds like us Reads like our past reports, no AI phrasing Pass Four out of five isn't a pass One start date came from the wrong line of the extract. The draft goes back, and the fix goes into the instructions: "take dates from the appointment line, never the filing date". "No invented facts" is always check number one. Each check is something a colleague could tick without asking you. Anything it can't find says [NOT IN SOURCE]. Anything it's unsure of says [CHECK]. Keep a line per run: date, minutes, errors found. In a month you'll know if it saves time

/session-3.h: Bring to session 4: Brief it once
/session-3.t: Next time we teach it to write like you. Bring samples of your own work, redacted or dummy. The more it sees of your real work, the closer it gets to how you write. Past work Two or three pieces you wrote for different clients. Before and after One set of source files and what you made from them. Your notes One piece of work you've already reviewed, with your notes on it. Brief and result One brief and the report or deliverable that came from it. This week: finish your scorecard and score one of your own recent pieces of work against it. Stuck on setup? Reply to any of our emails and we'll book a short one-to-one before the next session

/skill-file.t: Praxis · Standing instructions. Writing your skill file The most valuable thing you build with us is the rules. The script that runs them can be rewritten in an afternoon, but the rules are what a senior person in your role knows, written down so it stops living in one head. Takes about 5 minutes to read Then the evals guide, to prove the rules work

A plain Markdown file. There's no special syntax and no code, just prose and bullet points, the way you'd write a briefing note or a checklist for a new hire. It opens with a short header so anyone who reads it knows whose rules these are: Role: Due Diligence Analyst Use case: target company review memos Data types: company filings, auditor reports, news clippings Last updated: 2026-06-04 Then the rules

Rules are the things a senior person does automatically that a junior wouldn't know yet. It's the knowledge that isn't in any manual. Good rules are specific and you can test them. "Be thorough" doesn't tell anyone what to do. "Flag any supplier whose payment terms exceed 60 days" does. Start by asking yourself what would make you send a piece of work back. Those are your rules. Then ask what would make a client call to complain, and add those too. Here's a set for a BD analyst writing prospect research memos: Rules: - Lead with the decision. The first sentence is the recommendation. - Cite a source for every factual claim: (Source: [filename], p.[page]). - Flag any company that has changed leadership in the last 18 months. - Note if the company's stated headcount differs from LinkedIn estimates by more than 20%. - Use the client's language for their industry, e.g. "rig" for offshore, never "vessel". - Sections: Executive Summary, Company Overview, Key Risks, Recommended Next Steps. - Keep the Executive Summary to 3 sentences

Open Claude Code and start a conversation. Tell it your role, your use case and the task you want it to take on. Then ask: "Help me write the rules for [your task]. I want the kind of rules a senior [your role] follows that a new junior wouldn't know yet." It drafts something. Read it back and correct it. Take out anything generic and add the things from your field that only you would know. The version you end up with is yours. Then test it: could a competent person in your role read this file and produce work you'd be happy to sign off? If they couldn't, keep adding rules until they could

A common mistake is to write the skill file as a prompt, something to paste into a chat window and lose. It lives in your project folder, Claude reads it every time it does the job and Git keeps every version. When your rules change, and they will, you update the file and the next run picks up the new rules. Nobody has to remember to paste anything. It's also for the next person in your role, or for you in six months when you've forgotten why you wrote rule 7
A skill file tells Claude what good looks like. An eval checks that it actually got there, every time you change a rule. Read the evals guide. Tutto.One, daniel@tutto.one

/toolkit.t: Praxis · Setup. The Claude toolkit Claude on its own can read and write text. The extras on this page let it open a PDF, fill in a spreadsheet, read a scanned page or cut a recording, so here's everything on my machine, what each one does and which ones you need. Checked 3 Nov 2026 Start with the VS Code setup guide, then come back here Get it Worth having from day one Handy Add it when the job comes up Builders Only if you build apps or run servers

Add these in VS Code: open the Extensions panel (the four squares on the left), search for the name and check the publisher matches before you click Install. Copycat extensions with similar names do turn up. Claude Code anthropic.claude-code Claude in a panel beside your files. It reads the folder you have open, makes changes you can see and asks before it does anything big. Get it. PDF Preview tomoki1207.pdf Opens a PDF in a VS Code tab so you can check what Claude quotes without switching apps. Claude reads PDFs without it: this one is for you. Get it. Rainbow CSV mechatroner.rainbow-csv Colours each column of a CSV file so an export from Moodle, your CRM or a spreadsheet is readable before you hand it to Claude. Handy. YAML redhat.vscode-yaml Underlines mistakes in YAML, the format a lot of settings files and skill files use, so a missing space doesn't break them without you noticing. Handy. Remote SSH ms-vscode-remote.remote-ssh Opens a folder on another computer, a server for example, as if it were on your laptop. Claude then works on that machine. Comes with Remote SSH Editing and Remote Explorer. Builders. Dev Containers and Container Tools ms-vscode-remote.remote-containers · ms-azuretools.vscode-containers Runs a project inside Docker so it behaves the same on every machine, and lets you see what's running. Builders. Kubernetes ms-kubernetes-tools.vscode-kubernetes-tools For the client projects that run on a Kubernetes cluster. You won't need it. Builders. Also on my machine, you don't need these. Other AI assistants openai.chatgpt · google.gemini-cli-vscode-ide-companion · google.google-antigravity · mistralai.mistral-vibe-code I keep ChatGPT, Gemini and Mistral installed to compare them with Claude for clients. One assistant is plenty when you're learning. Builders. Claude Speak built by Tutto, so it isn't on the marketplace Reads Claude's answers aloud with the Mac's built-in voices. I built it for myself, so ask if you'd like a copy. Handy

These are small programs Claude runs behind the scenes when you ask it to do something. You rarely type them yourself: you ask, Claude runs the command and shows you what it did. Everyday. Python python3 The language Claude reaches for when a job needs real work on a file: totting up a spreadsheet, filling in a Word template, splitting a PDF. Most of what's in the Python section below runs on it. Get it. Git git Keeps a history of every change to a folder, so you can see what Claude changed and undo it. It's your safety net. Get it. Node.js node · npm · npx Runs a lot of the connectors that plug Claude into other apps, and the websites we build together. Handy. uv uv Installs Python and Python tools quickly and keeps each project's libraries separate, so one project can't break another. Handy. Homebrew brew The Mac's app store for command-line tools. One line installs anything else on this list. On Windows, winget does the same job. Handy. GitHub CLI gh Lets Claude save your work to GitHub, open a pull request or read an issue without you leaving VS Code. Handy. ripgrep and jq rg · jq ripgrep searches thousands of files in a second. jq reads and reshapes JSON, the format most apps export. Claude uses both to find things fast. Handy. Documents, scans and audio. Poppler pdftotext · pdftoppm Pulls the text out of a PDF and turns pages into images. Helps Claude with long or awkward PDFs. Handy. Tesseract tesseract · tesseract-lang Reads the words in a scan or a photo of a page (OCR), in many languages. Use it when a PDF is really a picture of a page. Handy. FFmpeg ffmpeg Cuts, joins, shrinks and converts audio and video. Claude uses it to trim a recording or pull the sound out of a video. Handy. whisper.cpp whisper-cli Turns a recording into a transcript on your own computer, so the audio never leaves it. Handy. For building and running apps. Docker docker Runs a database or a whole app in a sealed box on your laptop, so I can test a site before it goes live. Builders. Azure CLI and Supabase CLI az · supabase Talk to the cloud services some client projects run on. Builders. llama.cpp and Hugging Face CLI llama.cpp · hf Download and run open AI models on the laptop itself, for testing what works offline. Builders. browser-use browser-use (via uv) Lets an AI drive a web browser: click through a site, fill in a form, check a page works. Builders. LiveKit CLI livekit-cli For voice agents, the AI you can talk to on a call. Builders. Others codex · mistral-vibe · xc

Add-ons for Python. Each one teaches Claude to handle one kind of file properly, so it edits your actual Excel or Word file and the layout stays as you left it. Office files. openpyxl openpyxl · et_xmlfile Reads and writes Excel files, formulas and formatting included. This is how Claude fills in a spreadsheet you already have. Get it. python-docx python-docx Reads and writes Word documents: headings, tables, styles. Claude uses it to turn your guides into clean text and to fill in a template. Get it. ReportLab reportlab Makes new PDFs from scratch: certificates, handouts, a report in your colours. Handy. PDFs, scans and images. PyMuPDF PyMuPDF (imported as fitz) The fastest way to read, split, merge and search PDFs. It also pulls out the images and tells you which page a line is on. Get it. pdf2image and pytesseract pdf2image · pytesseract Turn PDF pages into pictures, then read the text in them. Together with Poppler and Tesseract above, this handles scanned documents. Handy. Pillow pillow Resizes, crops and converts images, screenshots for a handout for example. Handy. lxml lxml Reads HTML and XML quickly. Word and Excel files are XML inside, so the other libraries lean on it. Handy. Audio and the rest. Whisper openai-whisper · torch · tiktoken · numba · numpy The Python version of the transcriber above. It's a big download (torch alone is over a gigabyte), so only add it if you transcribe a lot. Handy. Requests requests · certifi · urllib3 · idna · charset-normalizer Fetches a web page or talks to an app's API. The four small ones come with it. Handy. Jinja2 Jinja2 · MarkupSafe Fills a template with your data, for example 30 personalised letters from one spreadsheet. Handy. SymPy and NetworkX sympy · mpmath · networkx Maths and maps of how things connect. They came in with other tools: you won't use them directly. Builders. Install the office and PDF set python3 -m pip install openpyxl python-docx PyMuPDF reportlab pdf2image pytesseract pillow On Windows type py in place of python3

/toolkit.h: The easy way to install any of this
/toolkit.t: Ask Claude. Type "Install openpyxl and python-docx so you can work with my Excel and Word files" into the Claude Code panel. It checks what you already have, runs the commands and asks before each one, so you can say no. Start with the ones marked Get it, then add the rest when a job needs them. If anything fails, copy the error into Claude or email me and we'll find 15 minutes. Tutto.One, daniel@tutto.one

/vscode-setup.t: Setup guide VS Code with Claude and Mistral From a fresh install to your first task with two AI agents. Six steps, each with the screen you should see. Updated. October 2026 Time needed. About 30 minutes Step 01

VS Code is a free editor from Microsoft. It is where Claude and Mistral will read and write your files. Go to code.visualstudio.com/download. Windows: download the User Installer and run it. Accept the licence, keep the default folder, leave Add to PATH ticked, then click Install and Finish. No admin rights needed. Mac: download the Universal build, open the.zip and drag Visual Studio Code into Applications. Open VS Code. You should see the empty window in Fig. 1. Step 02

/vscode-setup.h: Find your way around the screen
/vscode-setup.t: Three areas matter: the file navigator on the left, your files in the middle, and the AI panel on the right. Four buttons in the top-right corner show and hide them. 1 Fig. 1 A fresh window. Nothing is open yet. 1 The layout buttons, left to right: customise layout, left side bar (files), bottom panel (terminal), right side bar (AI chat). Click one to show it; click again to hide it. The left side bar holds the Explorer, your file navigator. Open a working folder before you start, so the agents know where to work. 1 2 3 Fig. 2 Explorer open, no folder chosen yet. 1 Explorer icon. Click to open the file navigator; click again to minimise it. 2 Open Folder. Pick or create a working folder for the session. 3 The left side bar button does the same as the Explorer icon. Shortcut ⌘B / Ctrl+B. Use a practice folder. Create an empty folder such as Desktop/New for training. Keep real case files out of it until the team is comfortable with how the agents behave. Step 03

/vscode-setup.h: Install the Claude and Mistral extensions
/vscode-setup.t: Both agents are free extensions. Many look-alikes exist, so check the publisher before you click Install. 1 2 Fig. 3 The Extensions view. Shortcut ⇧⌘X / Ctrl+Shift+X. 1 Extensions icon in the left-hand bar. 2 Search box. Type the extension name here. 1 2 3 Fig. 4 Search for claude and pick the official extension. 1 Claude Code for VS Code, published by Anthropic with a verified tick. Click Install. 2 Publisher: Anthropic, anthropic.com. 3 Identifier: anthropic.claude-code. Anything else is not the official extension. 1 2 3 Fig. 5 Search for mistral and pick Mistral Vibe. 1 Mistral Vibe VS Code, published by Mistral AI. Click Install. 2 Mistral Code is the older extension, shown struck through. Skip it. 3 Identifier: mistralai.mistral-vibe-code. Extension Publisher Identifier Sign-in Claude Code for VS Code. Anthropic. anthropic.claude-code. Paid Claude plan (Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise) or Claude Console account. Mistral Vibe VS Code. Mistral AI. mistralai.mistral-vibe-code. Mistral API key, pasted once during setup. Step 04

/vscode-setup.h: Open the AI panel on the right
/vscode-setup.t: Keep the agents in the right side bar. Files stay on the left and you can watch both at once. First, trust the folder that holds your work. VS Code opens any folder it doesn't know in Restricted Mode, and in Restricted Mode your extensions are switched off, so Claude and Mistral won't show up. Trust works on the parent folder: trust the folder that holds all your working folders and every folder inside it is trusted too, so the agents are there each time you open a new window. 1 2 Fig. 6 A folder opened in Restricted Mode. The right side bar only has the built-in Chat. 1 The Restricted Mode banner. If you see it, your extensions are off in this window. 2 Click Manage to open the Workspace Trust page. 1 2 3 Fig. 7 The Workspace Trust page. 1 What Restricted Mode costs you: here 23 extensions are off, the agents among them. 2 Trust switches everything on for the folder you have open. 3 Trusted Folders & Workspaces. Scroll down, click Add Folder and pick the parent folder, the one that holds all your working folders. Every folder inside it is then trusted too. 1 2 Fig. 8 Trusted. The banner has gone and the agents are back. 1 Claude Code and Mistral Vibe tabs in the right side bar. 2 The extension icons are back in the left-hand bar too. Pick the parent with care. Everything under a trusted folder can run tasks and extensions without asking. Trust the folder you keep your own work in, such as Desktop if your practice folder is Desktop/New. Don't trust Downloads or your whole home folder, because files from other people land there. Open the panel. 1 2 Fig. 9 The right side bar with one tab per agent. 1 Right side bar button. Click to open or minimise the AI panel. Shortcut ⌥⌘B / Ctrl+Alt+B. 2 One tab per agent. Click Claude Code or Mistral Vibe to switch between them. 1 2 Fig. 10 Mistral Vibe in the same panel. 1 Mistral Vibe tab. 2 Prompt box. Type your request here. If an agent opens on the left or as a tab in the middle, drag its tab into the right side bar. VS Code remembers the position next time. The first time you open each agent, it asks you to sign in (Claude) or paste your API key (Mistral). Sign in to Claude. You do this once. VS Code hands you over to your browser, you log in to your Claude account and approve the connection, then you come back to VS Code. 1 2 Fig. 11 The first time you open the Claude Code tab. 1 Claude.ai Subscription. Pick this if you have a Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise plan. 2 Anthropic Console. Only if your organisation pays f

/vscode-setup.h: Run a first task with Claude
/vscode-setup.t: Give Claude a task and watch the Explorer. New files appear on the left as Claude creates them. 1 2 Fig. 16 Before the task: an empty folder, and Claude's mode menu. 1 The open folder, still empty. 2 Modes. Manual asks before each edit; Plan explores first and shows a plan; Auto approves actions that pass a safety check. Switch with ⇧Tab. 1 2 Fig. 17 The prompt goes in. Claude starts checking the folder. 1 The request: a demo kit with a CLAUDE.md, a script and a basic tool for an investigator. 2 The Explorer is still empty while Claude plans. 1 2 Fig. 18 Seconds later the files appear in the navigator. 1 New in the Explorer: cases, sample_evidence, casekit.py, CLAUDE.md and demo.sh. Click any file to open it. 2 Markdown files open as raw text. Switch to Markdown Preview to read them formatted. 1 Fig. 19 CLAUDE.md formatted, and Claude's summary of what it built. 1 Claude reports what it made, what each file does and that it ran the demo end to end. 1 Fig. 20 Expand the folders to see everything the run produced. 1 A case folder with evidence files, a case record, a custody log and a report, all created by the task. CLAUDE.md is the briefing file. Claude reads it at the start of every session in that folder. Here it holds the commands and the rules: evidence goes in only through the tool, the custody log is append-only, and the kit is for lawful work only. Edit it to brief Claude on how your team works. Step 06

/vscode-setup.h: Run a task with Mistral Vibe
/vscode-setup.t: Mistral works on the same folder. Switch tabs and give it a task; here it builds a reusable skill from what Claude produced. 1 2 Fig. 21 Mistral reads the folder before it acts. 1 The request: assess the folder and create a skill for repeat work. 2 The live status line shows each command Mistral runs. 1 Fig. 22 The + menu. 1 Add context (point to a file), attach an image, run a command, or loop a task. 1 2 Fig. 23 Mistral's approval modes. 1 Ask requires approval for every action; Accept Edits approves file edits only; Smart Approve prompts only for risky actions; Auto Approve runs everything. 2 The current mode. Click to change it. Choose the approval mode on purpose. In these screenshots both agents run in Auto. That is fine in a practice folder. With real case material, use Manual in Claude and Ask in Mistral until you trust the workflow, so every command waits for your approval. In Fig. 21, Mistral reads files outside the open folder; agents can reach anything your user account can. Reference

Action Mac Windows Show / hide file Explorer (left). ⌘B. Ctrl+B. Show / hide AI panel (right). ⌥⌘B. Ctrl+Alt+B. Open Extensions. ⇧⌘X. Ctrl+Shift+X. Search every command. ⇧⌘P. Ctrl+Shift+P. Switch Claude's mode. ⇧Tab. Shift+Tab. If something is missing. No layout buttons: right-click the title bar and tick Layout Controls. Agents missing and a Restricted Mode banner at the top: the folder isn't trusted. Click Manage and trust its parent folder (Fig. 7). Extension installed but not showing: search every command for Developer: Reload Window. Claude says “Not logged in”: reload the window; the sign-in screen reopens. Mistral asks for a key every time: rerun setup from the Mistral Vibe panel and paste the key once. Sources. Custom layout, Microsoft VS Code docs. Use Claude Code in VS Code, Anthropic. Mistral Vibe for VS Code: install and authenticate, Mistral AI

/workspaces.t: Setup guide Share folders with VS Code workspaces Keep the folders you use again and again in one place on your computer, and link them into each project. Claude can still read them, and you stop copying the same files into every folder. Updated. November 2026 Time needed. About 5 minutes Before you start. VS Code setup guide Step 01

Most of us start by copying the same reference material into every new folder: the sample report, the instructions, the scorecard, the brand guide. It works, but it doesn't last. Say you open one folder per person you're researching, and each one gets its own copy of the sample report and your instruction files. After ten cases you have ten copies. Improve the instructions in one and the other nine are out of date, and your computer fills up with the same heavy files over and over. A workspace fixes that. Your project folder stays exactly as it is, and the shared folder stays where it lives. VS Code shows both side by side in the Explorer and remembers the link in one small file. Change the shared folder once and every workspace that links to it sees the change. Good candidates for a shared folder: your design system, a sample report you want Claude to copy the style of, scorecards, CLAUDE.md templates and skills. Anything you'd otherwise paste into every project. Step 02

/workspaces.h: Drag the shared folder into VS Code
/workspaces.t: Open your project folder in VS Code as usual. Then find the shared folder in Finder (or File Explorer on Windows) and drag it onto the Explorer panel on the left. 1 2 3 Fig. 1 Dragging a folder from Finder onto the Explorer. 1 The workspace. Here it's called Example and holds one folder so far, Example, which lives on the Desktop. 2 Example.code-workspace is the small file that remembers which folders belong to this workspace. You make it in step 5. 3 The shared folder on its way in. Drop it anywhere on the Explorer panel. Prefer menus? File, then Add Folder to Workspace… does the same thing and lets you pick the folder. Step 03

When you drop the folder, VS Code asks what you want to do with it. This is the one choice that matters. 1 2 Fig. 2 Copy it, or link it? 1 Add Folder to Workspace. Pick this one. VS Code links the folder and leaves it where it is. 2 Copy Folder makes another copy inside your project, which is exactly what we're trying to stop. VS Code may ask whether you trust the folder. Say yes only if it's your own material. If the shared folder sits inside the parent folder you trusted in the VS Code setup guide, it won't ask. Step 04

/workspaces.h: Check it's linked and not copied
/workspaces.t: The shared folder now shows up as a second folder at the top level of the Explorer, next to your project folder. 1 2 3 Fig. 3 Two folders, one workspace. 1 Your project folder, unchanged. 2 The shared folder, praxis-design-system, at the same level. 3 Hover over it to see where it really lives, here ~/Desktop/NB/praxis-design-system. Open the Example folder in Finder and you won't find it there. Add as many shared folders as you like. To take one out, right-click it and choose Remove Folder from Workspace. That only removes the link: the folder and its files stay where they are. Step 05

Until you save it, the workspace is called Untitled and VS Code forgets the links when you close the window. Close the window, or choose File, then Save Workspace As…. When VS Code asks whether to save your workspace configuration, click Save. Save it inside your project folder and give it the project's name. You get one extra file, such as Example.code-workspace (Fig. 1, box 2). It only holds the list of linked folders, nothing else. Next time, open that file instead of the folder: double-click it, or use File, then Open Workspace from File… All the linked folders come back with it. For a new project, open its folder, drag in the same shared folders and save a new workspace. One shared folder can sit in as many workspaces as you like. Step 06

/workspaces.h: Point Claude at the shared folder
/workspaces.t: Claude works the same way it did before. To make sure it uses the shared material, tell it where to look. Right-click the shared folder, or a file inside it, and choose Copy Path. Paste the path into your message in the Claude Code panel, for example: Write the report in the style of the sample in followed by the path. If Claude asks for permission to read the folder, allow it. Keep the shared folder light. Claude reads text far better than PDFs. Convert the reference PDFs you use most into Markdown or text files once, and keep those in the shared folder. Every project that links to it gets the faster, more accurate version. Reference

Drop it on the Explorer panel on the left. You clicked Copy Folder by mistake: delete the copy inside your project folder and drag the original in again. The linked folders are gone after a restart: you opened the project folder instead of the.code-workspace file. Open the file. /courses/00-praxis-start-here.html.h: Software is exact. AI is likely. Pair them
/courses/00-praxis-start-here.html.t: Software does what you tell it, the same way, every time. AI is different: it gives you answers based on probability, and it comes out a little different each time. Claude Code puts the two together. You say what you want in English, and it writes rules that then run the same way every time. Think of it as an Excel formula that now lives in your folder. The logic is captured once, and it repeats. 03 Tutto. The idea · the architecture The idea

/courses/00-praxis-start-here.html.t: Everything lives in a folder on your machine. The rules are written in plain English, the know-how is saved as a skill, a script does the repeating, and your files sit right next to them. You work in your own folders, not in the Claude app. There's no website to go down and no portal to break. Everything the system knows is in that folder, and the folder is yours. 04 Tutto. /courses/00-praxis-start-here.html.h: Don't ask for the answer. Ask for the thing that makes it
/courses/00-praxis-start-here.html.t: If you ask AI for an answer, you get a good one, but it's different every time. If you ask it to build the script that produces the answer, you now have something that runs the same way for the next thousand. That's the difference between using AI and building with it. This one move is behind every system on the next few screens. 05 Tutto. The proof The proof

/courses/00-praxis-start-here.html.h: Built, not bought. Starting with my own company
/courses/00-praxis-start-here.html.t: I run my own company on systems built this way: our books and events, and our outreach. The subscriptions they replaced are cancelled. We build the same way for clients. I'll show you three, and why they keep getting better. The best proof I have is that my own business runs on this. /courses/00-praxis-start-here.html.h: My company's books and events, with no subscription
/courses/00-praxis-start-here.html.t: An event or a job becomes a quote. The quote becomes an invoice. It goes out through our own email service and the books stay current. I cancelled the accounting package; this does the job and the data stays with me. No portal to log into, no monthly fee. We built it once and it runs every month. 07 Tutto. /courses/00-praxis-start-here.html.h: Sales that knows how to talk across borders
/courses/00-praxis-start-here.html.t: An emailing and intelligence system with its own dashboard. It drafts messages suited to how people communicate in each country, tracks the pipeline, and produces the reports and quotes I send straight to customers. /courses/00-praxis-start-here.html.h: One spec PDF in. Seventy-eight finished assets out
/courses/00-praxis-start-here.html.t: An e-commerce platform sends a spec for 78 asset formats. A script turns that PDF into a reusable set of rules, like one big spreadsheet formula, then produces all 78. Each comes back editable, so a person finishes the last ten percent. /courses/00-praxis-start-here.html.h: It gets better the more you use it
/courses/00-praxis-start-here.html.t: Not all 78 are perfect the first time. But the user shows the system what it got wrong, and the rules improve. Ten percent to fix becomes five percent, then one. The time you save grows every month. This is the real return. A bought tool is as good as it will ever be on day one. A system you teach keeps improving. 10 Tutto. /courses/00-praxis-start-here.html.h: One build becomes many. And it can stay private
/courses/00-praxis-start-here.html.t: Build it once for one case and you've built it for every case like it, whether that's ten or a hundred. And when the data is sensitive, the whole system can run on your own machine, where nothing leaves your network. The work you do once pays back on every case like it. And when the system runs on your own machine, the data never leaves the office, so confidentiality is a fact, not a promise. 11 Tutto. Your turn · where to start Your turn

/courses/00-praxis-start-here.html.h: How to find the one that's yours
/courses/00-praxis-start-here.html.t: You don't need a big strategy. Look for a task that ticks three boxes: it touches several systems, it repeats the same way every time, and it's costly when it's wrong. A task that ticks all three is where to start, and you can usually find one in an afternoon. What it costs: about twenty dollars a month. Expect it to get you ninety percent of the way; you finish the last ten by hand. The hard thing to find is a guide who has done it before, not the software. 12 Tutto. A better workflow: you bring context and judgement, then work on any problem together, with a system that understands and speaks your language: "intelligence". /courses/01-praxis-claude-101.html.h: Set the STAGE · Define the TASK · Specify the RULES

/courses/01-praxis-claude-101.html.h: When it's off, it's almost always fixable
/courses/01-praxis-claude-101.html.t: The first draft is a starting point. Most disappointing answers trace back to one thing: The prompt was missing something. Run a quick eval (5–10 of your own examples) to learn where Claude already fits your work. 05 Tutto. Lesson 4 · Meet Claude Lesson 4

/courses/01-praxis-claude-101.html.h: Three modes, matched to the size of the job
/courses/01-praxis-claude-101.html.t: The desktop app gives you one Claude in three shapes. Pick by how big and how hands-off the work is. Cowork and Code run on Claude Code underneath: local to your machine, able to spin up subagents and sustain long tasks. /courses/01-praxis-claude-101.html.t: Not a wall of code buried in the conversation. A finished thing in its own window: rendered, editable, ready to use / download. /courses/01-praxis-claude-101.html.t: A skill is a folder of instructions and resources Claude loads when it's relevant. Two kinds, and one clean rule of thumb. /courses/01-praxis-claude-101.html.t: Not a single lookup. Claude works agentically: planning, running many searches that build on each other, then writing it up with citations. Reach for Research when a thorough answer needs many sources. For a quick fact use web search; for pure reasoning use extended thinking; for internal-only questions use Enterprise Search. 12 Tutto. /courses/04-praxis-claude-code-in-action.h: A prompt is a request. A hook is a guarantee
/courses/04-praxis-claude-code-in-action.t: Asking Claude to "always run the formatter" is a request it might forget. A hook is a shell command that runs every time, no exceptions. /courses/05-praxis-ai-fluency-framework-.t: Practical techniques that turn a vague ask into a clear brief. Prompting is iterative, not one-shot; expect to refine. The shortcut most people miss: hand the AI your prompt and ask it to make it better. 11 Tutto. Lesson 10 · Competency Lesson 10

/courses/06-praxis-claude-with-the-anthr.h: One request, and the API forgets you
/courses/06-praxis-claude-with-the-anthr.t: You send a model, an optional system line, and the whole message list. It replies once. There's no memory. To continue, you append the reply and send it all again. A "multi-turn conversation" is just this loop run by hand: the model holds nothing between calls, so the growing messages[] list is the memory. Same key, same shape, whatever language you call from. Key concept Minimum request = model + messages + max_tokens in the body, API key in the headers. Keep the key in an env var /.env, never hardcoded. → teacher notes (incl. web-app: key stays server-side). 03 Tutto. Lesson 2 · Make the call Lesson 2

/courses/06-praxis-claude-with-the-anthr.h: Four dials on the same request
/courses/06-praxis-claude-with-the-anthr.t: You don't change the model to change the behaviour. You turn these. The system prompt does the heavy lifting. It's where the role and rules live. Temperature trades reliability for variety; streaming is about feel; structured output is how you get data a program can actually use. Key concept For clean JSON with no prose to strip, use forced tool use ( tool_choice ): define a tool whose schema is the shape you want, read back the validated object. → teacher notes (prefill+stop-sequences is the lighter, flat-JSON alternative). 04 Tutto. Lesson 3 · Make it reliable Lesson 3

/courses/06-praxis-claude-with-the-anthr.h: Stop guessing whether a prompt is good
/courses/06-praxis-claude-with-the-anthr.t: An eval is a test suite for prompts: a set of cases, run automatically, graded, scored. Change the prompt, re-run, watch the number move. Two ways to grade: code-based for anything exact (is it valid JSON? does it contain the answer?), model-based for judgement (is this tactful? is it on-topic?): you ask another Claude call to score it against a rubric. Key concept The eval loop: build test cases → Claude generates responses → grade them → score → refine and re-run. The step after generation is grading; model-based grading uses another AI to judge. → teacher notes. What's a "model grader"? The model-based half: another Claude call that scores an output against a rubric. The go-to when "right" is a judgement (tone, relevance, helpfulness) that code can't check exactly. How far do you trust it? Write a clear rubric, have it return a one-line reason with the score, and check it against human marks on a sample before you lean on it across hundreds of cases. 05 Tutto. Lesson 4 · Make it reliable Lesson 4

/courses/06-praxis-claude-with-the-anthr.h: Four techniques, in order of leverage
/courses/06-praxis-claude-with-the-anthr.t: When the output is wrong, you rarely need a bigger model. You need a clearer prompt. Reach for these in order. Examples (few-shot) move quality the most: a couple of worked input→output pairs teach format and edge cases that paragraphs of instruction can't. XML tags matter because Claude is trained to respect them: <document>…</document> reads cleaner than quotes. 06 Tutto. Lesson 5 · Extend its reach Lesson 5: if you take one thing away

/courses/06-praxis-claude-with-the-anthr.h: Tool use is a round trip you complete
/courses/06-praxis-claude-with-the-anthr.t: Claude can't run anything. It can only ask. You describe the tools; it replies "call this, with these arguments"; you run it and hand back the result; it continues. The loop can repeat. Claude can call several tools across several turns before it answers. This single mechanism is what every agent is built on: the model proposes, your environment executes, the result comes back. So a tool is a special Anthropic endpoint? No. There's one Messages endpoint. A tool is a plain function in your own code; Claude only ever returns a request to call it (name + arguments) and waits for your result. Is it a config file that sets Claude's behaviour? No. A tool is your code, plus a declaration (name, description, input schema) that tells Claude the function is available, not how it should behave. 07 Tutto. Lesson 6 · Extend its reach Lesson 6

/courses/06-praxis-claude-with-the-anthr.h: Some tools you don't have to build
/courses/06-praxis-claude-with-the-anthr.t: Most tools are yours to implement. A few ship with the API. You switch them on and Anthropic runs them server-side. The text editor and code execution tools are exactly what powers Claude Code and the analysis features. The Files API lets a request reference uploaded files (PDFs, datasets) without re-sending them every call. Key concept The code execution tool's main limit: it runs Python in an isolated sandbox with no network access. The Files API is the upload-once / reference-many store that also moves inputs in and outputs (charts) back out. → teacher notes. 08 Tutto. Lesson 7 · Extend its reach Lesson 7

/courses/06-praxis-claude-with-the-anthr.h: RAG: give it knowledge it was never trained on
/courses/06-praxis-claude-with-the-anthr.t: You can't fit a whole knowledge base in one prompt. So you index it once, then retrieve only the few chunks each question needs and paste them in. Embeddings catch meaning ("car" finds "vehicle"); BM25 catches exact terms (an error code, a part number). A multi-index pipeline runs both and merges the hits. That's what production RAG actually does. 09 Tutto. Lesson 8 · Extend its reach Lesson 8

/courses/06-praxis-claude-with-the-anthr.h: The same API takes more than text
/courses/06-praxis-claude-with-the-anthr.t: Four capabilities ride on the request you already know: two change what goes in, two change what comes out. Extended thinking gives the model room to work through hard problems before committing to an answer. Citations turn "trust me" into "here's the passage", the backbone of any answer a business has to stand behind. Key concept PDF vs image: a PDF is read as text and images (a document block, supports citations); an image is vision-only. PDFs cost more per page but give the richer, citable understanding. → teacher notes. 10 Tutto. Lesson 9 · Extend its reach Lesson 9

/courses/06-praxis-claude-with-the-anthr.h: Pay for the long part once
/courses/06-praxis-claude-with-the-anthr.t: Most prompts start with the same big block: a system prompt, tool definitions, a document. Cache that prefix and later calls read it instead of re-paying for it. The rule: only an exact, unchanged prefix is reused, so put everything stable first and the variable part last. Cache lifetimes are short (minutes), so it pays off across a burst of related calls, the heart of any responsive, repeated-context app. Key concept Caching needs two things: mark the block cache_control: ephemeral and clear the minimum length (~1,024 tokens on Sonnet 4.x, ~4,096 on Opus 4.5+). Under the minimum it silently runs uncached, with no error. → teacher notes. 11 Tutto. Lesson 10 · Build systems Lesson 10

/courses/06-praxis-claude-with-the-anthr.h: MCP: one standard plug for tools and data
/courses/06-praxis-claude-with-the-anthr.t: Without it, every app wires up every integration by hand. With it, a server exposes its capabilities once and any client can connect. A server publishes three things (tools, resources, prompts) and the inspector lets you test it before wiring it to a client. Build the integration once; plug it into Claude Code, your own client, or anyone else's. Exposing document contents? That's a resource: read-only data Claude can pull in. Actions it performs are tools; pre-tested instructions (like a formatter) are prompts. Defining a tool in Python? Easiest way is the @mcp.tool() decorator (FastMCP). The function's name, docstring and type hints become the tool, no schema by hand. How do client and server talk in dev? Almost always stdio: the client runs the server as a subprocess over stdin/stdout. No ports, no auth. HTTP is for remote. Why three primitives, not one? Different owners. Model picks tools, the app loads resources, the user invokes prompts, so each is offered the right way. 12 Tutto. Lesson 11 · Build systems Lesson 11

/courses/06-praxis-claude-with-the-anthr.h: Workflows vs agents: who decides the path
/courses/06-praxis-claude-with-the-anthr.t: Both chain LLM calls. The difference is control: in a workflow you wire the steps; in an agent the model chooses them as it goes. Choose by predictability. If you can draw the steps in advance, a workflow is cheaper and more reliable. If the path depends on what's found along the way, you need an agent. Claude Code is one. Most production systems mix both. Want it to handle the unexpected? Give the agent a few general tools and let it pick, not one narrow tool per case you predicted. General tools recombine into paths you never scripted. One long prompt it keeps half-ignoring? Chain it. Split the rules across a few small steps so each call holds less, and check the output between them. 13 Tutto. Praxis The whole thing, in one line Make the call. Trust it. Give it reach. Compose it into systems. A stateless request is the unit. Evals and prompting make it reliable; tools, RAG and the model's own capabilities give it reach; MCP and the workflow-vs-agent choice are how you build something real. tutto.one/praxis · daniel@tutto.one. 14 ← → or space · F11 fullscreen

/courses/07-praxis-introduction-to-model.h: Host, client, server: one client per server
/courses/07-praxis-introduction-to-model.t: The app you use is the host. Inside it, each client holds one connection to one server, and the server wraps the real tool or data. Messages travel as JSON-RPC over a transport: stdio for a local server, HTTP for a remote one. The host can hold many clients at once, but each client talks to exactly one server. What does each side hold? The server offers the capabilities: tools, resources, prompts. The client is the connection that reaches one server and brokers them to the host. Supplier vs. connector. Is the client one shared pipe? No: one client per server. The host opens a separate, named line to each server, so you grant and revoke them one at a time. 04 Tutto. Lesson 3 · Foundation Lesson 3

/courses/07-praxis-introduction-to-model.h: A server is a few lines to start
/courses/07-praxis-introduction-to-model.t: The Python SDK's FastMCP does the protocol plumbing. You create a server, register capabilities, and run it over a transport. stdio runs the server as a local subprocess of the host; HTTP exposes it as a remote service. Same server code either way; the transport is just how messages travel. What does "transport-agnostic" mean? MCP fixes the language, not the channel. The JSON-RPC messages are identical whether they ride a local stdio pipe or an HTTP connection; neither side's logic changes. Rewrite the server to go remote? No. Its tools, resources and prompts stay the same; you swap the transport (stdio → HTTP), not the code. 05 Tutto. Lesson 4 · Tools Lesson 4

/courses/07-praxis-introduction-to-model.h: Tools: actions the model can choose to call
/courses/07-praxis-introduction-to-model.t: Decorate a function and its name, docstring and typed arguments become a schema the model reads. The model decides when to use it. A clear name and description matter: that text is all the model has to decide whether and how to call the tool. Treat the docstring as a prompt, not a comment. 06 Tutto. Lesson 5 · Tools Lesson 5

/courses/07-praxis-introduction-to-model.h: Test the server before wiring it to an app
/courses/07-praxis-introduction-to-model.t: The Inspector connects straight to your server, no LLM involved. List what it exposes, call each tool by hand, read the raw response. Debug the server on its own first. If the Inspector can list and call everything cleanly, the problem later is in the client wiring, not the server. 07 Tutto. Lesson 6 · Tools Lesson 6

/courses/07-praxis-introduction-to-model.h: The client feeds tools to the model, in a loop
/courses/07-praxis-introduction-to-model.t: Your client lists the server's tools, hands their schemas to Claude, runs whatever Claude asks for, and feeds the result back, until it has an answer. This is the same agentic loop a chat window doesn't have: the model can act, see the result, and decide what to do next. MCP is just how the tools get there. 08 Tutto. Lesson 7 · Resources & prompts Lesson 7

/courses/07-praxis-introduction-to-model.h: Resources: data to pull in, addressed by URI
/courses/07-praxis-introduction-to-model.t: Read-only data the server exposes at an address. No side effects: think GET, not POST. A URI scheme like docs:// names the data. Direct resources return a collection; templated ones take a parameter to fetch exactly one: a single document, a single record. 09 Tutto. Lesson 8 · Resources & prompts Lesson 8

/courses/07-praxis-introduction-to-model.h: The app decides which resources to load
/courses/07-praxis-introduction-to-model.t: Unlike tools, the model doesn't reach for resources. The application (often the user) chooses what context to bring in. That's the difference from a tool: a tool is the model's to call, a resource is the app's to load. Same server, two different control models, which is the heart of MCP. 10 Tutto. Lesson 9 · Resources & prompts Lesson 9

/courses/07-praxis-introduction-to-model.h: Prompts: reusable templates the author ships
/courses/07-praxis-introduction-to-model.t: A tested, parameterized prompt the server exposes, so the right wording is baked in instead of reinvented every time. Prompts move hard-won phrasing out of people's heads and into the server. The author tunes it once; everyone else just calls it and gets the good version. 11 Tutto. Lesson 10 · Resources & prompts Lesson 10

The client lists the server's prompts and offers them to the user. Pick one, fill the arguments, and it expands into the full message. If you've used a slash command in Claude Code, you've used an MCP prompt. The server ships the command; the client makes it a one-keystroke action. 12 Tutto. Lesson 11 · Recap Lesson 11: if you take one thing away

The whole protocol, in one picture: what the server exposes, and who gets to trigger each one. Everything in the course hangs off this: tools the model calls, resources the app loads, prompts the user triggers. Get the owners straight and the rest follows. 13 Tutto. Praxis The whole thing, in one line One protocol. Three primitives. Any tool, any app. Tools, resources and prompts, exposed by a server and reached by a client inside your host, so context and capability plug in once instead of being rebuilt every time. tutto.one/praxis · daniel@tutto.one. 14 ← → or space · F11 fullscreen

/courses/08-praxis-introduction-to-agent.t: Four moves: grasp the idea, build one, place it among the other tools and share it, then fix it when it misbehaves. What it is. 1 What a skill is. Build one. 2 Your first skill. 3 Config & multi-file. Fit & ship. 4 Skills vs other tools. 5 Sharing skills. Fix it. 6 Troubleshooting. 02 Tutto. Lesson 1 · What it is Lesson 1: if you take one thing away

/courses/08-praxis-introduction-to-agent.h: If you keep explaining it, write it down once
/courses/08-praxis-introduction-to-agent.t: A skill is a folder of instructions. Claude holds only its one-line description until your request matches, then it loads the rest. Personal skills ( ~/.claude/skills ) follow you across every project; project skills (.claude/skills ) ship in the repo for the whole team. The rule of thumb: if you find yourself repeating an instruction, that's a skill waiting to be written. 03 Tutto. Lesson 2 · Build one Lesson 2

Create a directory, write SKILL.md, restart. Claude loads every skill's name and description at startup, then matches your request to them. Claude loads only names and descriptions at startup, then asks you to confirm before pulling the full skill into context. If two skills share a name, priority decides, so keep names distinct. 04 Tutto. Lesson 3 · Build one Lesson 3

/courses/08-praxis-introduction-to-agent.h: Keep SKILL.md lean: split the rest out
/courses/08-praxis-introduction-to-agent.t: Two fields are required, two optional. Past about 500 lines, move detail into supporting files Claude opens only when it needs them. allowed-tools fences a skill (say Read, Grep, Glob, Bash only) for read-only or sensitive work. And tell Claude to run a script, not read it: the source never enters context, only the result does. 05 Tutto. Lesson 4 · Fit & ship Lesson 4

Skills load on demand when your request matches. The other four solve different problems. Pick by when each one fires. Reach for a skill when knowledge should apply automatically the moment the topic comes up. CLAUDE.md is always-on standards; subagents isolate delegated work; hooks fire on events; MCP brings in outside tools. Most setups use several at once. 06 Tutto. Lesson 5 · Fit & ship Lesson 5

/courses/08-praxis-introduction-to-agent.h: Three ways to share: widest reach last
/courses/08-praxis-introduction-to-agent.t: Commit to the repo for your team, publish a plugin for the community, or push enterprise-managed settings for the whole organisation. One gotcha: subagents start with a clean context, so they don't inherit your skills. List them in a custom agent's skills: field. Built-in agents (Explore, Plan, Verify) can't use skills at all. 07 Tutto. Lesson 6 · Fix it Lesson 6

/courses/08-praxis-introduction-to-agent.h: When it breaks, it's one of five things
/courses/08-praxis-introduction-to-agent.t: Run the validator first. Then match the symptom to its fix. Most "won't trigger" problems are just the description. Test the exact phrases you'd type ("why is this slow", "make this faster") and add any that fail to the description. That single fix solves most triggering problems. Run claude --debug to see loading errors by name. 08 Tutto. Praxis The whole thing, in one line Write it once. Describe it well. Let Claude load it when it fits. A folder and a SKILL.md turn a repeated instruction into automatic, shareable expertise: built lean, placed among the other tools, fixed by its description. tutto.one/praxis · daniel@tutto.one. 09 ← → or space · F11 fullscreen

Build. 2 Creating one with /agents. Design. 3 Designing it well. Judgment. 4 When to reach for it. 02 Tutto. Lesson 1 · Concept Lesson 1

/courses/09-praxis-introduction-to-subag.h: A subagent works in its own context
/courses/09-praxis-introduction-to-subag.t: It gets a role and a task, does the messy work out of sight, and hands back only the answer. Built in already: a general-purpose agent, Explore for fast search, and Plan for plan-mode research. The tradeoff: you lose sight of how it got there. 03 Tutto. Lesson 2 · Build Lesson 2

/courses/09-praxis-introduction-to-subag.h: Make one with /agents: Claude writes the file
/courses/09-praxis-introduction-to-subag.t: Describe what you want; Claude generates the name, description and system prompt. It's a markdown file with a short YAML header. Scope it project-level (this repo) or user-level (everywhere). Put the word "proactively" in the description and Claude will delegate without being asked. 04 Tutto. Lesson 3 · Design Lesson 3

/courses/09-praxis-introduction-to-subag.h: Four things separate a worker from a wanderer
/courses/09-praxis-introduction-to-subag.t: A good subagent is steered by its description, knows when to stop, reports what it hit, and touches only what it must. The description does double duty: it decides when the subagent launches and shapes the task prompt the main agent writes for it. Vague in, vague out. 05 Tutto. Lesson 4 · Judgment Lesson 4: if you take one thing away

That one question decides it. If you don't need to watch the journey, delegate. If you do, keep it in your main thread. Why code review makes the list: Claude critiques code more honestly when it didn't write it. A fresh-context reviewer beats asking the thread that built the feature. 06 Tutto. Praxis The whole thing, in one line Isolate the work. Shape the output. Delegate by judgment. A subagent runs in its own context and returns a summary. Build it with /agents, steer it with a sharp description and an output format, and reach for it only when the journey doesn't matter. tutto.one/praxis · daniel@tutto.one. 07 ← → or space · F11 fullscreen

Nine ideas, one per screen: a small, clear model of the machine. Each is a thing to point at while you explain. The drama is in the watching, so take the silences. 01 Tutto. The shape of the course Where we're going

/courses/10-praxis-ai-capabilities-and-l.h: The whole course on one screen
/courses/10-praxis-ai-capabilities-and-l.t: Four moves: what generative AI is, how its character forms, the four properties that bound it, and the calibrated trust they add up to. What AI is. 1 Two halves of one system. 2 Four properties, one continuum. How it forms. 3 Character: pretrain + fine-tune. The four properties. 4 Next Token Prediction. 5 Knowledge. 6 Working Memory. 7 Steerability. Calibrated trust. 8 When properties collide. 9 Locate the task. 02 Tutto. Lesson 1 · What AI is Lesson 1

The 4D Framework teaches how you work with AI. This course teaches how AI works with you: the machine properties those human competencies respond to. Why it's durable: the boundaries move as models improve, but the properties stay the same. Learn the shape once and it keeps paying off. 03 Tutto. Lesson 2 · What AI is Lesson 2: if you take one thing away

AI isn't uniformly clever or uniformly unreliable. It's strong and weak along four predictable axes, and the same mechanism gives you both ends. Calibrated trust isn't trusting or distrusting AI wholesale. It's locating your task on each continuum, then matching how hard you check to where it sits. 04 Tutto. Lesson 3 · How it forms Lesson 3

/courses/10-praxis-ai-capabilities-and-l.h: Character is trained in, not emergent
/courses/10-praxis-ai-capabilities-and-l.t: Politeness, helpfulness and caution don't appear by magic. Two training stages build them, and each leaves predictable fingerprints. Preface a request with a wrong assumption ("I think this plan is bulletproof") and watch it validate you. That's sycophancy, and once you can name it, you can see it coming. 05 Tutto. Lesson 4 · The four properties Lesson 4

AI writes word by word, by what tends to follow what. That single mechanism gives you both the fluency and the fabrication. The "text your friend" demo makes it visceral: keep tapping your phone's suggested word and you've built a tiny language model. Fluency and fabrication are the same mechanism. You can't have one without the other. 06 Tutto. Lesson 5 · The four properties Lesson 5

/courses/10-praxis-ai-capabilities-and-l.h: It knows what it read, frozen at a cutoff
/courses/10-praxis-ai-capabilities-and-l.t: No live browsing by default, no lived experience, a hard stop at the training cutoff. The real question isn't "does it know this?" but "how well-represented was this in what it read?". Characteristic failures: staleness, uneven coverage, inherited bias in what counts as "normal," and no memory of its sources. The 1024-dimension demo shows how retrieval finds meaning, not keywords: "car" lands near "my Civic needs brakes.". 07 Tutto. Lesson 6 · The four properties Lesson 6

/courses/10-praxis-ai-capabilities-and-l.h: The middle of a long context gets lost
/courses/10-praxis-ai-capabilities-and-l.t: Everything the AI attends to lives in a fixed window. Attention weights the edges. What lands in the middle quietly disappears. It's a cliff, not a gradient: it works until it doesn't, and the overflow is silent. The fix isn't more context, it's smarter: front-load, repeat what matters, start fresh. Memory, compaction and projects push the cliff out. 08 Tutto. Lesson 7 · The four properties Lesson 7

/courses/10-praxis-ai-capabilities-and-l.h: It follows the letter, not the spirit
/courses/10-praxis-ai-capabilities-and-l.t: The model follows instructions the way it does everything: by continuing a pattern. That makes it steerable, and leaves a gap between what you said and what you meant. When it's followed literally but uselessly, restate the goal; saying it louder won't help. "Shorter, so the exec sees the ask on page two" lands right. In multi-step work, insert a checkpoint so an early slip doesn't carry to the end. 09 Tutto. Lesson 8 · Calibrated trust Lesson 8

/courses/10-praxis-ai-capabilities-and-l.h: Most failures are two properties meeting
/courses/10-praxis-ai-capabilities-and-l.t: Real-world trouble is rarely one property acting up. Name the two that collided, and the fix points itself out. Other pairs work the same way: confidently wrong math (offload it to code), an agreeable bad premise (invite genuine pushback). Naming the pair is Discernment applied: you evaluate better when you know what kind of wrong you're looking at. 10 Tutto. Lesson 9 · Calibrated trust Lesson 9

/courses/10-praxis-ai-capabilities-and-l.h: Hold a small model of the machine
/courses/10-praxis-ai-capabilities-and-l.t: Fluent use isn't memorising every failure mode. It's recognising which kind of wrong you're looking at, and reaching for the matching response. That's calibrated trust, and it survives every model upgrade. This course is the machine half; the 4D Framework & Foundations course is the human half that acts on it. 11 Tutto. Praxis The whole thing, in one line Four properties. Each a continuum. Trust, calibrated. Next Token Prediction, Knowledge, Working Memory, Steerability: locate your task on each, then match how hard you check to where it sits. tutto.one/praxis · daniel@tutto.one. 12 ← → or space · F11 fullscreen

https://claude.ai/artifact/S7dHFnALQxEY3.h: The 8 steps, and what you fill in
https://claude.ai/artifact/S7dHFnALQxEY3.t: Each week builds on the one before, so the rules come first and every later step works inside them. Week 1 Rules first: your AI charter, first draft. Week 2 Define good: your use case card, 2 or 3 redacted example reports, then a scorecard for each recurring job. Week 3 Which tool, and what to hand over: the hand-over check for your task. Week 4 Brief it once: 3 samples of your own writing, so it learns your house style. Week 5 Tools: one template you reuse, with placeholders instead of real names. Week 6 Check it before it ships: one AI draft put through the checking routine. Week 7 Skills and automation: a colleague tries one of your skills. Week 8 Agents, and what comes next: your first agent, and the list of bigger jobs.

1. Which tools and accounts can be used for client work? Paid accounts only, with training switched off. Free accounts for public information only. A login several people share means everyone sees everyone's chats. 2. Can a client's name go in? No. Write the client and paste the brief with names and identifying details removed. 3. Can an interview verbatim go in? Yes, once the source is Source A and anything that could identify them is removed. Target names can stay, in an approved account. 4. Criminal, health or other sensitive findings about a target? Only what the brief needs, only in an approved account and always read by a person before it reaches the client. Check with your lawyer or DPO how GDPR (Articles 9 and 10) applies. 5. Content from social media profiles that aren't public? Stays out of AI tools until agreed with your lawyer. Public posts can be screened against your keyword list. 6. Results from people-search tools and paid databases? Check each provider's terms first. 7. Connections to email, Google Drive or SharePoint? None until week 5, and then only to folders without live client files. 8. Who checks AI work before a client sees it? The person who signs the report reads every AI-drafted line against the source. 9. Do clients get told when AI was used? Italy's AI law (Law 132/2025) asks professionals to tell clients. Agree one sentence for your engagement letter or reports. 10. What if someone isn't sure, or a rule gets broken? Ask Alice before. If it already happened, tell Alice the same day. Nobody gets blamed for reporting it.
In ChatGPT it's Settings, Data controls, Improve the model for everyone. In Claude it's Settings, Privacy, Help improve Claude. Free accounts have the same switch, so turn it off there too.

https://claude.ai/artifact/S7dHFnALQxEY3.h: After the call: finish your charter
https://claude.ai/artifact/S7dHFnALQxEY3.t: Choose How our people use AI and How we govern and oversee AI. Background Italia Srl, Italy, which brings in GDPR, the EU AI Act and Law 132/2025. List where you already use AI: adverse media checks, translation, summarising articles and documents, cross-checking findings, polishing reports and interview write-ups. Say who approves a new tool, who people ask when they're not sure and who signs off client work. Review every 6 months.

/ai-charter.t: Answer the questions section by section: what the charter covers, your organisation, vision and principles, people and governance, commitments and rollout, keeping it current. It writes the charter for you to download. Your answers stay in your browser, so finish on the same computer you start on. Choosing Italy brings in GDPR, the EU AI Act and Law 132/2025.

/use-case-card.t: About 20 minutes for one real task: who it's for, what goes in, the steps you take today, what good output looks like and what must never happen. Open it from your dashboard so it saves to your account. Use dummy or redacted details.

/agent-scorecard.t: Pick a recurring job and write the checks every draft has to pass: accuracy against the source, completeness, tone, format, what must never appear. Each check gets a pass mark. Use it to score AI drafts and your own work the same way. There is also a version you can give to any AI assistant.

/handover-list.t: For one task, decide what AI should do, what it shouldn't, and what it needs to run without you: the inputs, the rules and the check at the end. There is also a version you can give to any AI assistant.
